speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EFFECT UPON EXISTING WAR CONTRACTS OF INCREASES IN MINIMUM WAGE RATES
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Labour with respect to an order in council reported to have been passed on May 31 providing for increases in minimum wage rates for the manufacture of supplies for the government, and providing that government contractors must now pay not less than the rates set up under the law of the province where the work is performed and never less than 35 cents per hour for adult male employees and 25 cents per hour for adult female employees. This is said to be retroactive in effect.
Having regard to the steady rise in the cost of living I am in accord with the principle underlying this announcement. I understand it is felt that the minimum wage paid in certain cities in the province of Quebec is too low. The question arises: Does this order in council apply to all contracts let by the government on a competitive basis, and if it is to be retroactive in effect, is it the intention of the government that the difference in cost occasioned thereby in respect of competitive contracts let prior to the passing of the order in council will be made good by the government, or will the contractor be obliged to make good the difference?

Commonwealth Air Training

subtopic: EFFECT UPON EXISTING WAR CONTRACTS OF INCREASES IN MINIMUM WAGE RATES
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. I think the use of the word "retroactive" has proven to be a little misleading, and if I read section 2 of the order in council it might answer his question:	It reads:
The terms of all existing contracts of the type to which the said "B" conditions apply, shall be revised by the insertion therein of the foregoing schedule of minimum wages, such revision to become effective ten days after written notice thereof has been communicated to the contractor.
I think it would be a fair interpretation to say that this applies to all new contracts and to other contracts in connection with which notice has been given pursuant to the terms of the order in council. I shall table the order in council. I think any adjustments will have to be considered not by the Department of Labour but rather by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). speechtext: I should like to put a question to the government based upon a news item which appeared in most of the Canadian newspapers during the last week-end. speechtext:
I have been expecting for some days that a question like this would be raised, and I have had in my portfolio a letter which I received from the high commissioner of the United Kingdom in reference to the matter to which my hon. friend has just referred. The letter is dated May 13, 1941, addressed to myself as Secretary of State for External Affairs, and reads:
My dear Prime Minister,
I am writing about the proposal that the United Kingdom government should avail themselves of certain facilities for civil flying training in the United States of America, which Sir Archibald Sinclair discussed with Colonel Ralston at the time of the latter's visit to London.
The United Kingdom government are grateful for the Canadian government's cooperation in the consultations on the subject which have proceeded between the two governments since, and are glad that there is agreement that the proposal offers advantages that we should unhesitatingly accept. The United Kingdom government wish me to repeat at the same time that these plans will in no way reduce the scope of the joint air training plan in Canada, wrhieh, together with those other measures of assistance in the field of air training so generously afforded by the Canadian government, are being developed much beyond the maximum degree originally planned and at a pace which is far ahead of the original schedule. This constitutes a remarkable achievement by the Canadian authorities who are mainly responsible for this scheme, which will, we believe, be one of the most weighty and decisive factors in gaining victory for our arms.
Yours sincerely,
Malcolm MacDonald.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CHEESE FOR SHIPMENT TO BRITAIN-CANADA TO SUPPLEMENT BASIC PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement on behalf of the dairy products board.
The agreement between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom completed on the 31st October, 1940, provides that Canada will supply the United Kingdom Ministry of Food with 112,000,000 pounds of cheese manufactured during the year ending March, 1942. The United Kingdom Ministry of Food has agreed to accept such additional quantities as may be available for export. The price to be paid by the United Kingdom Ministry of Food is 14-4 cents per pound on board ship eastern Canadian ports. The government of Canada has supplemented this to the extent of -6 cents per pound, making a basic price of 15 cents per pound for first grade cheese on board ship.
The dairy products board on the 20th May, 1941, issued an order requiring that during an indefinite period commencing 26th May, 1941, all cheese manufactured in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are to be large white cheese and to be exported.
The dominion government is supplementing the price of cheese for export to the extent of another cent per pound, making a basic price on board ship of 16 cents for first grade cheese. This extra price will be applicable to cheese manufactured on and after the 26th day of May and exported. The dominion government is, therefore, supplementing the amount paid by the United Kingdom to the extent of 1-6 cents per pound.
On a basis of the minimum quantity to be exported, namely, 112,000,000 pounds, Canada's contribution at 1-6 cents per pound amounts to $1,792,000, but if the quantity actually exported exceeds 112,000,000 pounds this amount will be increased by 1-6 cents per pound on each pound over 112,000,000 which is exported.

On section 17-Gasoline.

Mr. Chairman, I was unavoidably absent when this question

was previously before the house, and for that reason I should like to speak on this item at this time.
I have received a large number of protests against the imposition of the gasoline tax so far as agriculture is concerned, in that it means an increase in the cost of production for the western farmer at a time when the government is doing nothing to assure him of a fair return for the products which he sells. Every other industry but agriculture is in the position of receiving a fair return. I was surprised to read all the arguments advanced by the Minister of Agriculture for supporting this tax. At page 3052 of Hansard he said:
It is a tax which, even as now proposed, is levied on a very small percentage of the farmers of Canada.
So that his justification was that only a few were affected thereby. At page 3054 he set out the reasons why he was supporting this tax. I quote:
Coming to the question whether this tax should be imposed on farmers, or whether there should be any tax on farmers, I think we shall all agree that the farmer does pay his share of taxation, whether this three-cent tax is imposed or not. I am not arguing the question from that point of view at all. A three-cent tax on gasoline does mean something to many farmers. It does not mean as much as some of us would seem to have convinced ourselves that it does with regard to many farmers of certain types.
A little further down he says:
But I think I am in agreement with at least sixty per cent, and probably seventy-five per cent, of the membership of this house when I say there never has been introduced in this house a budget which was so completely a farmers' budget as the budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance. That is recognized by farmers all across Canada.
He refers to the budget as a farmer's budget. No doubt he has some reasons for making that statement. If I understand it correctly it means this, that it is a farmer's budget because of the fact that in the main it imposes increased income taxes; and by reason of the operation of the policies of this government and its failure to assure the farmer an income, there being therefore no income, it is a farmer's budget for which the government should be commended.
No one is arguing against any of the taxes in this budget on the basis that the people of Canada are not willing to pay them. I realize the difficulty which confronts the Minister of Finance in raising taxes; I appreciate the necessity of securing revenue. But the best way for the minister to make a success of the campaign for the loan which is now before the people of Canada would be to go on the radio and assure the people

Special War Revenue Act
that their sacrifices and their willingness to make them are appreciated, and that this government is going to cut out unnecessary expenditure for non-war purposes and pare down necessary ones to the limit.
A return has been made to the house this very day in connection with which I wish to protest in that it shows that the governmenat is continuing to increase nonwar expenditures at a time when ever-increasing taxation is being imposed upon the people. Referring to the Minister of Agriculture's new policy for reducing wheat acreage by summer-fallowing, according to this return, which was brought down in reply to my question whether he had any men out in western Canada explaining the scheme, the Minister of Agriculture has thirty-seven men going about the country, each at a salary of $150 a month, plus living expenses when away from headquarters and mileage for use of cars, explaining to the western farmer the need of this legislation. Is there any justification for it at a time like this, I ask the Minister of Finance? Instead of reducing nonessential, non-war expenditures, one department alone proceeds with an expenditure of about $6,000 a month in order to explain to the farmer what he already knows through advertisements which have appeared in the press.
I suggest this-and I have not spoken before in reference to these various measures introduced by the Minister of Finance that when you expect people to make sacrifices so as to be able to contribute to the war loan, and when you impose taxation such as this upon the farmer, non-war expenditures should be reduced to the greatest possible extent, and it is difficult to see that this is being done.
In looking over the list of these expenditures I find that for the years 1938 to 1941 the estimated amounts of expenditure were approximately as follows, the year in each case ending on March 31: 1938, $125 millions; 1939, $411 millions; 1940, $455 millions; 1941, $434 millions, and the estimated expenditure for the year ending March 31, 1942, is $431 millions.

In two of those years we
had two sets of estimates, the main estimates and the special supplementary estimates, and then a third set, the ordinary supplementaries. I believe the hon. gentleman has compared the main estimates only in those two years with the main estimates of the last two years. We had only two sets of estimates in the last two years, as distinguished from three previously. I think the hon. gentleman has fallen into an error in his comparisons.

No, I am taking
the same set of figures all the way through,
and I am asking the Minister of Finance what is being done to reduce non-war expenditures. Apparently they have not been reduced more than a few millions. I find instances such as this which came to hand to-day, of thousands of dollars being expended in order to create jobs for friends in western Canada. There is no justification for this sort of thing.
I appreciate the industry which the minister applies to his position, and I assure him that if he would- tell the people of Canada that the estimates before the committee, and those to be brought down during the next few days, will be very considerably reduced, it would make a great deal of difference to the success of the loan campaign. As one example, take the Montreal terminal. The expenditure on that project in the coming year, in order to carry into effect a political promise, will amount to $4,466,596. I plead with the minister that political promises be not honoured in these times. I plead with him, so far as political promissory notes are concerned, either to extend the time for maturity or cancel them altogether.
Here we are in the last few days of the session, asking people to submit to ever-increasing taxation, which they are prepared to do for war purposes but not for controllable non-war expenditures. We as members of this committee have the right to protest against the government's having held back most of the non-war estimates until a time when, with termination of the session pretty well set for the end of the week, it will be impossible for us to deal with each one individually and give it the attention it should receive. The people are asking us to give these matters attention. They are willing to make sacrifices, but they expect us to see to it that the slogan "business as usual" is not to be applied to, or made an excuse for, continuing non-war expenditures at the amounts at which they now stand.
All over western Canada the farmers are asking that they be exempted from the gasoline tax. I have not at any time, in the committee or in the house, spoken in protest against any other tax. I recognize that taxation is necessary, but this particular tax is, in my opinion, most unfair. The Minister of Finance, in his argument, admitted it. He conceded its unfairness by saying that he had considered various avenues of escape, but that, because it would be difficult to arrange for exemptions, no course was open to him other than to put it into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that if we had had exemptions we would have had a considerably higher tax.

Yes, but the minister also said that the reason the farmers and
335S
Special War Revenue Act

fishermen were not exempt was that he, his colleagues and those associated with him, could not find any effective means of preventing evasions. He pointed to the situation in one province-he must have referred to Saskatchewan-and the difficulty of enforcing the ' provincial legislation as to refunds of gasoline tax.
I am registering my protest. I realize that our protests do not mean much, but I protest against the tax, and in doing so, I couple with it the suggestion that the minister immediately see to it that non-war expenditures be reduced, so that there may be no question of the performance of political promises at a time like this.
Now that we are trying to get tourists from the United States, the effect of this tax will be particularly undesirable. All over the United States, although I speak particularly of the west, the people are being warned by nazi propagandists not to come to Canada. All kinds of reasons are given, such as alleged difficulties at the boundary and interference with free ingress and egress. A recent article in the Financial Post shows that one of the chief arguments used against tourists coming to Canada, thereby providing us with United States dollars, is the fact that the Minister of Finance, on the occasion of the conference on the Sirois report, warned the Canadian people that rationing gasoline might be necessary. By increasing the tax you keep out more tourists. Within the last week I have had letters from people in the United States who regularly visit Canada, stating that in view of this tax they do not intend to do so any more.
In connection with the acquiring of United States dollars, here is an advertisement on behalf of the Canadian government which to my mind is the most unusual and peculiar which has ever been put out on behalf of Canada. It is issued by the Canadian government travel bureau in the United States and appears in the April issue of National Geographic magazine. What a description of Canada's war effort! I quote:
_ Canada at war is still the greatest playground in the world.
The word "still" is underlined. This is an advertisement that is to bring tourists into Canada! I ask for exemption, first, for farmers and, second, for tourists in order that United States dollars which we need shall not be diminished in their flow into Canada through reduction in tourist traffic consequent on the imposition of this tax.

I do not think I should let this opportunity pass without once more

protesting against this tax on gasoline as it applies to farmers and fishermen. I have already referred to the good times which have been enjoyed by industry. Labour is now enjoying the level of remuneration that prevailed between 1926 and 1929. If the farmers were receiving to-day the price for their wheat that they received at that time, they would be in a better position to face this tax. If we were getting the price paid between 1926 and 1929 we should be receiving $1.35 a bushel for No. 1 northern at Fort William, but instead of that we are getting 70 cents. Why are farmers singled out for unjust taxation when the prices they receive for their products are so unfair? One-third of Canada's population is on the land, and a large proportion of the people are directly dependent upon the farmers for their living. Why, then, are we discriminated against?
In the last analysis, farmers are the ones who have to bear the brunt of Canada's taxation. They are asked to send their sons to fight the battle overseas, and we want to know why we are discriminated against not only in the matter of prices but also in the matter of taxation. I am not speaking for the farmers of my constituency alone but for farmers across Canada, because it appears that a number of farmer representatives do not think it worth while protesting. My voice may not have any effect on the government's programme, but I think as a farmer representative I should at least protest against a tax which I regard as unjust.
What is the estimated revenue from the farmers through this gasoline tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no estimate.
Can the minister give no estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Even on the basis of the number of tractor farmers there are in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Has the minister given further thought to the representations which I and others have made, that farmers and fishermen be exempt from the gasoline tax? If the minister has not been able to do so as a federal measure, has he communicated with the provincial government to see whether a further rebate can be allowed to farmers and fishermen in Nova Scotia so that they will not have to pay more for their gasoline? They will be subject to

Special War Revenue Act
the highest gasoline tax in all Canada, and they are the people who are least able to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The farmers and fishermen in their work will pay the three cents in Nova Scotia just as others anywhere else will. It is the same, because there is an exemption of farmers and fishermen from the gasoline tax in Nova Scotia, apart from this impost.

I was asking whether any representations had been made to the effect that as a contribution to the war and a special concession to the farmers and fishermen in Nova Scotia in carrying on their vocations, there be an allowance by the province so that these classes of users would be relieved of the new tax on a commodity which is so essential in their occupations.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean that we should suggest to the government of Nova Scotia that they should make a rebate of part or all of the gasoline tax on gasoline used by farmers and fishermen for pleasure purposes?
I did not say that. I said, in their occupations as farmers and fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that respect they are now exempt.
Does the minister suggest that this three-cent tax does not apply to the farmers and fishermen in that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but the hon. gentleman has asked whether I would make representations to the government of Nova Scotia for a refund or some exemption from the tax on farmers and fishermen. They have no tax except a tax on gasoline used for pleasure purposes. That is why I asked the hon. member whether he wanted me to make representations for a remission of part of that tax.

I suggest that representations might be made by the minister to the government of Nova Scotia whereby the classes of users of gasoline in that province to whom I have referred might be compensated for this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not made any such representations. I am not sure I understand what they are, but I have not made them.

I protested against this tax when we were discussing the resolution and I do not intend to go over the arguments again. Since then, however, the minister has made the statement that this tax will affect only
a small percentage of farmers. I do not agree with him. It will certainly affect 90 per cent of the farmers of Canada, because there is not a farmer to-day who is not using gasoline for some purpose. He uses it in his threshing and other work as well. In western Canada last fall the cost of operations increased and the farmer absorbed that additional expense. With this added cost on gasoline, and with the wage increase that will come again this fall, the extra burden will be passed on to the farmers. This gasoline tax will be passed on to every farmer both in the west and in the east.
We have a shortage of agricultural products in practically every line except wheat. The Minister of Agriculture has announced that the price of cheese has been raised a cent a pound, the object being to promote greater production. We shall be faced this winter with a shortage of other dairy products, and in this tax we are putting an additional cost on the farmer which will tend to diminish his production of these things. I protest against this addition to the cost of agricultural production in Canada, when not only we but the people of Great Britain as well need the things that we can produce.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I might direct attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and make what I am sure he will agree is a necessary correction. The questions asked were these: How many persons are employed by the federal Department of Agriculture in explaining the summer-fallow bonus system in the three western provinces? What are their names? What remuneration and expenses does each receive? The answer is as follows:	At the present
time, thirty-seven persons are employed in field work in connection with the wheat acreage reduction programme in the western provinces. That work does not consist of just what my hon. friend referred to a few moments ago, explaining the summer-fallow bonus system. I have before me a list of those persons. I am not familiar with all the names, but I would say that with the exception of possibly half a dozen all these men were already in the employ of the federal government or of one or other of the provincial governments. That is, they were either in the employ of this government under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act or the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, or they have been in the employ of the government of one of the provinces in connection with relief matters, or in similar work among the farmers of that province. Those who have come from other governments have been given leave of absence for the time they will be working for this
Special War Revenue Act

government, which may be only a few weeks. The others, who have been employed in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, will carry on some of their previous activities in conjunction with the work they do in reference to the wheat acreage reduction. In other words, as I explained to the house earlier this session, the prairie farm assistance organization is being used for the purpose of administering the wheat acreage reduction plan; and many of the persons whose names appear in this list were employed in connection with our other activities, but are being paid for the time being under this appropriation.
What is the total number of completely new employees, and what is the total expense in respect of them?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not entirely familiar with these names, so that I am not in a position to say exactly how many of the thirty-seven are new, but my estimate would be that probably not more than half a dozen new men are on the list. The others are men who have been employed in these other activities. The total expense while they are doing this work will be at the rate of $150 per month per man. We do not know yet how long they will be on this work, but it will be for some weeks during the summer while seeding and summer-fallow operations are being carried on.
Would $2,000 or $3,000 cover it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would judge so. I should think that my hon. friend, in giving his figures a few moments ago, probably multiplied twelve by $150 and then by thirty-seven, but of course the total will not be anything like that amount.
The minister says there are six new employees.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Do not make it too specific; I am not absolutely sure, but it is about that number.
Does that include those who were formerly in the employ of the provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No; there are about six in addition to those formerly in the service of the dominion or provincial governments.
I think only about five or six of these men were with the provincial governments.
Then we have about six men who are new employees and another six who were formerly with the provincial governments, and who therefore would not be on the dominion payroll.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.
Then how many more were formerly employed under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Some of them.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would have to check the list to say. I am not sure of the number, but the remainder would be employed under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and in similar activities.

Would those
formerly connected with the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be in the service of the dominion government at the present time, as Prairie Farm Assistance Act employees?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Those who are employed under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are only called up for a few weeks during the summer. They are not what you might call permanent employees. So that these men who are designated as employees under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act have not been in the employ of the dominion government in recent months?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not want this converted into a discussion of agriculture estimates. Certainly it is out of order to discuss in detail the question which has been raised. I try not to raise points of order, but we are on the gasoline tax, and apparently we are in for an afternoon of discussion on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, or wheat reduction, or something of the kind.

I concur in what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said with regard to criticisms. We have appealed to the minister to remit this tax as it applies to farmers and fishermen. The other evening I

Special War Revenue Act
said the minister was stubborn. Perhaps that was not the word to use; possibly I should have said he is determined. In any ease it would appear that while this is a tax which the farmer and the fisherman should not be called upon to bear, the government is determined to impose it. Hon. members should realize that when our farmers are being asked to reduce their income by reducing their production, this additional burden will become almost a tragedy for a large number of those who are trying to carry on their operations. I just want to make this one further protest, because I am well aware of the fact that at this stage at least, it is useless to make an appeal.

When we were discussing this matter in the resolution stage I protested against the imposition of this tax. Already a good deal of time has been taken up in a discussion of the matter. It was considered on May 20, 21 and 22; and up to the evening of May 21 practically every hon. member who had taken part in the discussion had spoken against the imposition of this tax on farmers and fishermen. On May 22 the Liberals had a caucus, and apparently the members were whipped into line, because after that we had no further protests from that party.
One cannot help feeling that it is futile to oppose anything brought into the house by this government, even though the majority of hon. members may be against it. It is not a very nice criticism to have to offer against a so-called democratic institution, but apparently members are compelled to vote against their conscience or against the wishes of their constituents. During the whole debate the minister has not given one sound reason why exemption should not be granted in respect of coloured gasoline for agricultural purposes. There would be no possibility of abuse, and there would be no trouble about refunds. The Minister of Agriculture used a peculiar argument when he said there would not be more than 57,000 tractors in western Canada burning gasoline, and that therefore the problem would not be of very great importance. I suggest to him that 57,000 farmers have a right to expect from this house just and equitable treatment. On the other hand if his figures are correct it is an argument in the opposite direction, because if only 57,000 farmers are to be affected, the amount of revenue lost by the exemption would not be very great.
The hon. member for Portneuf said that the average amount of gasoline used by a farmer would not be more than 300 gallons a year. Of course that statement is incorrect. It may be true for Ontario, but in my own 14873-213
case, for instance, on a farm of not more than average size, I use anywhere from 1,500 to 1,600 gallons a season. That is very different from 300 gallons; it means an additional tax of about $45 or $50 each season. Multiply that by 57,000 and it will be found that these farmers will be compelled to contribute over $2,000,000 each year. It is a contribution they should not be called upon to make.
I say again to the minister that if it is a question of raising revenue, and if he feels that the government cannot do without the revenue, let him tap other sources which can be taxed with far greater justice. Again I suggest that one of those sources is advertising.

Section agreed to.
Section 18 agreed to.
On section 19-Building materials excluded.

When the resolution was before the committee I brought to its attention the serious shortage of housing in Brantford. Since that time I have returned to Brantford, and have had further interviews with his worship the mayor and members of the city council. I am informed that the housing situation in Brantford is indeed acute. I understand that the mayor is almost besieged by residents of Brantford who are about to be evicted or who have received notices advising them that they must move on or before a certain day. Unfortunately many of these people are wives of soldiers who are not now in Brantford. The situation is most distressing. To-day there are not enough houses in Brantford to accommodate the working people of that great industrial centre. Most of those people are engaged in essential war industries. I assume it is agreed that those employed in such industries should be housed under proper conditions.
Yesterday I read in the New York Times the following notation from Washington:
The United States Housing authority approved to-day a $2,896,000 contract to M. S. Kelliher Company of Boston for construction of 744 homes in Orchard Park, Boston. It also approved a $2,620,000 contract to Psaty & Fuhrman, Inc., of New York, for 744_ homes in the Roger Williams Homes Project at Providence.
This shows that in the United States, as in Canada, in many centres there are not enough houses to accommodate the working population.
When the resolution was before the committee I suggested there might be two ways of assisting the building trades in connection with low-cost housing. I asked whether it would be possible to remit the tax on building materials put into low-cost houses. I under-
Special War Revenue Act

stand that here an administrative problem might arise, but I should like to know whether it can be done. Further, the National Housing Act might be widened so as to allow a maximum loan on a house costing $3,000. The act provides that a maximum loan up to ninety per cent may be allowed on housing which costs $2,500 or less, including the price of the land. My information is that it is impossible to build a house to-day for $2,500. An additional sales tax has been imposed, and there have been some further increases in costs. I am informed that if the figure of $2,500 were stepped up to $3,000, the number of houses built would be increased. I leave these two suggestions with the minister. I cannot impress upon him too strongly the very great shortage of houses which prevails in Brantford, as I understand, it does also in other parts of Canada.

I wish to
join with the hon. member for Brantford City in expressing my regret that the government has felt it wise to place this tax on the building industries. I have expressed my disappointment with regard to the tax on children's theatre tickets and the tax on gasoline used by farmers and fishermen. This, however, I regard as the most regrettable and unfortunate tax imposed by the minister, and I hope it is not yet too late for him to reconsider it.
In recent years this government, and I believe most of the provincial governments, have encouraged the ownership of property and the building of small houses. Over a period of years many millions of dollars of government money have been spent to encourage the ownership of property by citizens of Canada. All will agree that the ownership of property by citizens is the very basis of contentment in any country. It has been the established policy of governments in Canada to encourage the people to build their own homes. In recent years in many parts of Canada, including Nova Scotia, it has not been practicable from the point of view of investment to build the workman type of house, or to invest in farm properties. It is very desirable that people should live in their own homes and have ownership of the property in their own right. This tax will make it impossible for many people to do that.
The hon. member for Brantford City has pointed out the scarcity of low-cost houses in that city. The same condition applies to many places in Nova Scotia. There is a great scarcity of workmen's houses in Halifax, New Glasgow, Sydney, Yarmouth, Amherst, Springhill and other centres. The minister

stated-I believe these are his figures-that he expected this tax would bring in a revenue of $15,000,000. This will mean taxation of almost $200,000,000 worth of building construction. Some building will not be affected because it is financed by the government. The tax will be payable by the government, increasing the cost of the properties. To that extent it is unsound and at the cessation of hostilities the government will have high cost property and suffer a substantial loss because this eight per cent tax has been imposed.
In the old days people who had money invested it in land and buildings and farms. That is not done to-day because the ownership of such property is a liability rather than an asset, except for those who occupy it. To-day they invest in bonds. Those who desire to own their own homes or farms should not have to pay this 8 per cent tax on building materials to provide or improve their houses or barns or farm buildings. In Nova Scotia there is still unemployment, and many people who might otherwise be able to obtain employment in the construction of new residences will not be able to do so because of this tax. Employment of that kind will be discouraged. From the point of view of the municipalities, it is essential that there should be as much building as possible by present and prospective home owners. It increases the assessments and makes for a contented people.
The encouragement of building is most important from the point of view of the lumber producers. In eastern Canada the lumber industry is in a difficult condition because of inability to ship overseas due to the scarcity of tonnage. A large quantity of lumber is available for construction, but the heavy tax of 8 per cent will discourage such work or make it impossible for people to proceed with the building of new homes and making improvements that they have had in mind. I join with the hon. member for Brantford City and other hon. members in expressing regret at the imposition of this tax and I ask the minister to reconsider the matter. He is obtaining some additional revenue from the increased tax on amusements, and he should cancel this tax or place it elsewhere. As the hon. member for Acadia has just suggested, he should listen to the appeal made by hon. members of this house, by the working men of Canada and by the municipalities; he should cancel this tax upon building materials, a tax which is most unjustifiable under existing conditions.

Mr. Chairman, it was with great regret that I noted the removal of the exemption of building materials from sales tax. I do not intend to

Special War Revenue Act
traverse the ground covered by the hon. member for Brantford City and the hon. member for Cumberland. I reaffirm the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Cumberland, that a country of home owners is the ideal thing. I am glad to be able to tell the committee that this principle prevails in my county, where the majority of houses are owned by the people living therein. Last year there was a substantial increase in the number of houses built in Fredericton. When I returned from the Easter vacation after the budget had been brought down and this exemption had been removed, my information was that a substantial number of people who had contemplated building had cancelled their arrangements. When I was home a week ago Saturday I was informed that for the first time in a number of years not a single house was being built in the city.
If the minister cannot go the whole way with respect to this, I suggest that he can at least go part way. In 1929 and all through the depression years there was a considerable amount of what I would call deferred maintenance. This condition continued through 1937, 1938 and 1939, and it is only in the last two years that people have begun to repair their buildings. I think the minister could have made an exception in the case of building materials used in the repair of homes or of properties rented as homes. These exemptions could have been limited to fairly small invoices, which would have the effect of allowing repairs long overdue to be made. I realize that there might be some difficulty in administration.
We know that such items as sashes and doors and so on are made in wood-working factories to-day, and not on the job as was the case a few years ago. I suppose these factories will have to take out licences under the sales tax provisions, and it would be easy to arrange for exemptions on comparatively small invoices covering materials for repairs to houses. In many parts of Canada buildings have been allowed to become dilapidated because their owners have been out of work and could not afford to carry out repairs. It is a sad commentary to go through the countryside and see how dilapidated many farm buildings are. I think the minister could have made some accommodation such as I have indicated.
The minister has wiped out all the exemptions. We all know the difficult times faced by the construction industry during the depression. Nothing gave the former government more concern than the fact that a large number of competent mechanics, such as carpenters and bricklayers, found it impossible to make 14873-213i
a livelihood. One of the reasons why the former prime minister and the former minister of finance established a government building scheme and started a housing scheme even in a small way was to give an impetus to the building trades of Canada. I believe, that had a good effect. But that forward step is now to be wiped out. For the first time in many years people have steady employment and are contemplating making repairs upoD their buildings, but they think twice now before carrying out their plans in that regard.
In one instance a group of men owned a vacant property in a certain community. A chain store company wished to establish itself in that community, and arrangements had been made and a loan from an insurance company actually negotiated to build the property that was to be rented to this company. This tax came on and added $8,000 to the cost of construction, and the whole deal fell through. I can give the minister the particulars if he so desires. There is one building that will not go on. This is regressive taxation of a very serious kind. The instance I have related was in connection with a property that was to cost $100,000. I am not pleading for that class of property to-day because I do not think we should embark on large or fairly large enterprises of that kind now, but I am pleading for the small home owner who for the first time has had a steady job in years and now has a little surplus money with which to put a new roof on his house, or to make necessary repairs. This tax is penalizing him. I ask the minister to reconsider it, if it is not too late.

I too ask the minister to reconsider this tax. I realize that there are administrative difficulties in exempting material for repairs or to be used in building modest houses for working people and people in the lower income groups. But I suggest to the minister that probably the time has arrived when in this matter, as in the manufacture of automobiles and some other things, the government should say that construction of houses of the luxurious type will not be permitted, and that the labour and material, if it is to be used at all for civilian purposes, shall be used for those who need housing and homes.
As the hon. member for Brantford City, the hon. member for Cumberland, and the leader of the opposition have said, housing conditions across this country are deplorable. I recollect that in my own city of Regina in 1931, when the census was taken, we were told that the average number of persons per room was two, and I am told by those who
Special War Revenue Act

live there now that the crowded condition in Regina, owing to concentration because of the war, is even worse than it was then.
I brought upon myself a little criticism the other day because I referred to conditions which I saw in the city of Halifax, Nova Scotia. I said that years ago I had visited the slums of the great metropolis of London, England, and spent several days in going through them, but that I had never seen anything worse there than I saw in the city of Halifax, Nova Scotia. There were crowded thousands and thousands of our people. One of the newspapers in Halifax said that I did not know Halifax, that my knowledge of the city was so limited as to preclude any authoritative statement, and that of course is true; but I did happen to be piloted around the city by someone who is an authority and I did see its slums.
Where were they?
On Maynard street, Market street, Argyle street, Grafton street and a number of other streets I visited.
You know your Halifax.

Yes, I have been there before. I would tell the hon. member for Halifax this, that in one place on Maynard street I saw something so shocking that I have never seen anything worse in my life- six or seven houses opening on a very small yard not nearly in length the width of this chamber, and in that yard, upon which there were dilapidated and filthy houses crowded with people, there was one small shed and under the same roof a common toilet and common water supply for all the people inhabiting those six or seven houses.
What would be the total number of places such as the hon. member describes in the city of Halifax?

I could not say. I hope at least that that kind of thing is found only infrequently. But the very fact that people have been living in Halifax under those conditions and that the municipal authorities have allowed them to exist in the middle of the city is a blot on the administration of Halifax.
I have a report here of the Nova Scotia Housing Commission for the year ended November 30, 1939. I am going to read just one paragraph from page thirteen. The report says:
The survey showed that of the number of places inspected-

This was in the city of Halifax alone.
-122 were unfit for habitation, in addition to 12 basements; while the number which did not conform to proper housing conditions was 129. The number of places considered unsuitable for human occupancy unless improved was 50. A total of 18 places which had been repaired were still not regarded as satisfactory. Only 4 places were recommended as suitable for habitation. Close to 3,000 people are living under conditions which are not satisfactory, the largest percentage of whom are existing under shocking conditions-the housing situation in Halifax is far more serious than perhaps it has ever been.
That was before the war was under way and before the city became crowded1. The government is making the gravest error at this time in placing an additional burden on the building of low-cost homes. The health of our people in the final analysis is our greatest asset, and no people living under conditions of this sort can be healthy. What is the use of building tuberculosis sanatoria, hospitals, and so on, if we allow housing conditions to exist in our cities such as I have described and such as this report indicates?
I am urging the minister to reconsider this proposal. If he must impose a tax-and he must, of course, somewhere else if exemptions are granted-then, if administrative difficulties are in the way, let the government prohibit the building of luxurious and extravagant houses. I cannot say that a $2,500 house ought to be the limit that should be permitted to be built at this time, because building costs vary in different parts of Canada. In some western cities it would cost from $4,500 to $5,000 to build a house that could be built for at least two-thirds of that amount in Ontario. But I believe a plan could be worked out of at least introducing some system of priorities in order to see to it that the health of our people is not impaired by a lack of housing, and this applies particularly to housing in places such as I have mentioned. I know that the government has been considering a plan for housing in Halifax and some other places, but I have not seen any definite announcement as to whether building has actually been authorized in that city.
There are other places besides Halifax dt is true; I have mentioned Halifax because I saw the conditions there and was criticized for having expressed my opinion as a result of what I saw. I know it to be the truth, and incidentally this report bears it out. The government should not discourage the building of modest houses, because poor housing interferes not only with the health but with the morals of the community. I certainly concur in what the hon. member for Brantford City, the hon. member for Cumberland and the leader of the opposition have said in regard to this matter.

I should like to add my voice to that of hon. members who have just spoken, in regard to the unwisdom of removing this exemption. I approve of everything which has been said by the hon. member for Brantford City. I have had some experience in the problem of housing, having spent some months in 1934 in a study of housing conditions in the city of Toronto. I regret to have to say that. I was charged with having cast an unnecessary slur upon Toronto in respect of its housing conditions. But after an investigation of many months we found that the slums there, although limited to small areas, were as bad as any I have seen in the city of London, where, some few years ago, I passed several weeks in investigating housing and slum conditions.
I strongly approve of the housing act which this government put into force in 1935. The act facilitated the building of a great many houses. The chief drawback, in my opinion, was that it did not go far enough; it failed to make provision for the low income group, those who could not afford houses costing more than, say, $1,500. The difference between that amount and the actual cost of the house will have to be taken care of by somebody. In my opinion it is the combined responsibility of the municipality, the provincial and the dominion governments.
A few years ago Mr. Purvis made a report on this subject. I commend particularly to the attention of all hon. members the appendix to that report dealing with low-cost housing, and I hope the time will come when those recommendations will be implemented.
In his own department the Minister of Finance has an excellent branch, headed by Mr. Nicolls, who have done splendid work. As I said a few months ago in this chamber, the work of this group should be extended and more money provided to enable them to prepare plans to deal with the situation after the war. When our soldiers come home from overseas it will be too bad if they have to settle down amid the slum conditions which, I am afraid, some of them left to serve their country. If we intend to take care of this very important post-war work we should begin now. It will require several years of careful planning to be ready to go ahead with it when it is most needed.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke of the health conditions associated with poor housing. I can confirm what he said. We found such cases as that of one person with tuberculosis sleeping in a room
with children who were susceptible to the disease and who would, I have no doubt, in the course of a few months, contract the disease. Another serious aspect of the housing problem is overcrowding. It was not an unusual experience to find three or four different families occupying the same house, with one family to a room. One can understand that this has a bad moral effect. Such slum districts are frequently centres where crime is bred; for children are forced to spend their time in the streets where they soon learn to gang up with other children and thus often become centres of criminal activity.
I shall not dwell further on this subject. I merely suggest to the minister that he should find some means of maintaining this exemption for the cheaper houses, say those which cost in our province $3,000 to construct, as suggested by the hon. member for Brantford City. It may be necessary in the west to raise the exemption to a higher figure. The leader of the opposition made a very good suggestion when he pressed for the exemption from the tax on lumber and materials for repairs. I hope that the minister will give this matter his very careful and sympathetic consideration.

It is not my intention to protest to-day against this tax, because, as the minister knows, I did so on May 5 and May 22. Because this country does need houses for its working men. Speaking on May 22 I urged the minister to consider this proposal from the point of view of giving the working man something to work for, so that he would have a home of his own. I do not know whether the minister has built a house for himself, but if he has he will know there is great pleasure in doing it. These workmen get much pleasure out of it, and it makes them better citizens. On May 22 the minister said:
Now it is desirable for them to make the old house do, as far as they possibly can, so as to leave the steel for the radiators free-if it is steel.
Commenting on that the other day, a man remarked to me that he did not think the minister should have said that, when this

I have just a word or two to say. I have been a director for fifteen to twenty years of the Toronto housing company. That company is a semi-philanthropic institution: 15 per cent of the stock was paid in, and the bonds were guaranteed by the city of Toronto up to 85 per cent of their value. In Toronto we have a large property comprising about 350 apartments ranging from one room to apartments of six rooms. They serve a definite purpose and rent at from about $20 a month up to $45. What worries me is the cost of keeping up the repairs on such properties. The majority of them were built in 1913, so that they are getting fairly old. We have kept them in good shape, but repairs on that property will probably cost from $20,000 to $30,000 a year. The result is that the tax on material going into those repairs will run from $1,600 to S2,400 a year, and that means that we shall have to raise the rents. Not only that, but the city of Toronto had to come to the assistance of the housing company, and they urge that we keep the rents down. I mention the Toronto housing company as an illustration to show that many houses in Toronto which are of the same age must be kept up, and this tax will affect them. Whether the tax goes on or not, material will have to be bought for repairs so as to enable people to live in these houses.
I doubt whether it is the intention of the minister to tax repairs to properties in this

way. There is an increasing demand for houses, and in the centres of these cities there are houses that can very well be made over. The home improvement plan was something that gave impetus to the making over of old houses so as to render them habitable. Although the money for the home improvement plan is out, there is an opportunity for people to do the same work without the assistance of the government, but it seems to me to be quite a burden to ask them to pay eight per cent on the cost of the work. It is all to the advantage of cities that are growing, if people try to retain the population within the city instead of having it spread to the outskirts. It saves overhead. But people will not pay an added eight per cent tax on repairs to old houses. I do not believe it is the minister's intention that they should. Without the assistance of the national housing act, workmen and others can put up small houses because their incomes are greater. I think it would be better if the tax were limited to houses not exceeding $3,000. There should not be a tax on material going into such houses, nor should the tax apply to repairs to apartment buildings. Repairs must be kept up. In Toronto there is a by-law that authorizes the city to compel the repairing of any house. It is a hardship to be obliged to repair a house and to pay the extra tax on it. I wish the minister would reconsider the eight per cent sales tax on repairs of this kind.

Hon. members have discussed this problem from various angles, particularly the scarcity of houses and the question of encouraging people to own their own homes. The question has also been discussed of improving what in some cases are deplorable living conditions. In these sentiments I must express complete concurrence. I would emphasize one thing that has not been discussed extensively so far and that is the position of those who are employed in and expect to continue in the construction industry. I would also consider the subject from the point of view of the unemployment problem on the western prairies. Out there we have not yet received any appreciable amount of work through the efforts of this administration, although a number of us from the prairies have urged upon the government from time to time the advisability of taking advantage of the resources of man-power and material in that section of the country. In addition to that, under the present policy introduced in connection with wheat, the income of the prairie provinces has been considerably reduced. In fact, this year it will be less than fifty per cent of what it was last year. Gener-

Many people in western Canada and particularly in the prairies have been depending on the increased activity in construction to bring them employment. I would point out to the minister what I interpret as two objects of the legislation which in my opinion do not apply to the prairies. In the first place, I presume that one reason for a tax like this would be that man-power is required in other industries, particularly war industries, but so far as the west is concerned, the government has not seen fit to take advantage of our man-power there, and therefore that object for the legislation is not applicable. The second object, as I see it, is revenue; and again, so far as the prairies are concerned, this tax, according to what I am informed by those who know the building industry better than I do, will almost completely retard any progress in construction out there. I know the city of Halifax almost as well as does the hon. member from that city, and I am sure that the housing condition has been understated. That general condition cannot be viewed from the driveway here in Ottawa; it must be analysed as a whole.
I wish to bring to the minister's attention a problem in my section of the country with which I am familiar. When, about thirty years ago, coal mining developed in Nova Scotia, a community was built up round the mines with housing accommodation sufficient to accommodate about 50 per cent of the men employed in and around the mine. Houses in these mining sections are absolutely deplorable. In the eastern end of Nova Scotia the only improvements in housing have been made by individuals who have endeavoured to secure pieces of land, to erect houses on them, and thus to maintain their families. A good deal of that has been done in the last two years.
In addition to that, the housing problem has been dealt with by cooperative organizations in that part of the country. The provincial government has cooperated to the extent of inaugurating a housing programme whereby groups are formed. These groups, each of which consists of twelve men, secure pieces of land. Through the medium of their credit union, sufficient money is raised to make down payments on the land. Eighty per cent of the total cost of the building is lent by the provincial government.
Five groups have been organized which have completed their homes. The amount allowed for each home is $1,800. Each man must build his own home; that is, he must draw the plans and build the house. I know of many groups which are prepared to go ahead this summer with buildings of that kind, thereby solving for themselves the housing problem existing in mining communities. Whole villages are being created in this way. They can put up such a building for $1,800; but if a contractor were hired, the cost would be $3,500. This additional tax of 8 per cent upon the lumber will cost them $144. The only cost entering into the house is that of material, the labour being all done by themselves.

The hon. member for Acadia was a little severe upon those who may vote for this measure notwithstanding the arguments which have been advanced against it. There is a compulsion upon hon. members on this side of the house which is greater than that imposed upon hon. members on the other side. Hon. members on this side are responsible, through the committee of council which they support, for the carrying on of the war effort. It is true that members of the opposition also have responsibilities in that regard, but not in the same intimate way.
That is a new theory; we all have equal responsibility.

I am glad the hon. gentleman feels that he has a responsibility. I wondered sometimes whether that responsibility was realized. Perhaps it should be there, and to that extent I withdraw my remark. There rests, however, upon the shoulders of hon. members on this side of the house who support the administration, a responsibility which others may claim if they so desire. What is the compulsion? It is the compulsion resting upon the Minister of Finance to provide the funds with which to carry on this war effort. It is the belief of members on both sides of the house, with some few exceptions, that this money should be raised by the orthodox and traditional methods of
taxation which have been in vogue in this country for a number of years. Some hon. members do not always realize their evil effects. I hold a certain view in connection with these methods of taxation, which increase the cost of living, check production and tend towards poverty among our people. I think it is perhaps a little less objectionable than tariff taxes, but it is a destructive tax on 'business, one which checks building, checks buying, increases the cost of living and tends towards poverty. They destroy morality and family ties. They destroy the basis of society itself by their destruction of self-respect and their promotion of delinquency and crime.
That committee examined as many as 1,332 dwellings, and their summary shows that 96 per cent, not of all dwellings but of those 1,332 dwellings, fell below the minimum standard of amenities; 75 per cent of those dwellings fell below the minimum health standard, and 55 per cent of them were verminous. There is nothing that can be said on the floor of this house in criticism of the housing conditions of our cities which would be extravagant or overstated. And, Mr. Chairman, the finest excuse for this tax which I have yet heard voiced from the floor of this house is

that it was designed for the purpose of stopping building. That was the expressed purpose of the Minister of Finance.

Large
building.

No; I do not think so. I think the minister went all the way because the tax goes all the way-8 per cent. I congratulate him upon not increasing the sales tax. I cannot congratulate him upon the extension of the sales tax, for it has for its purpose the stopping of building as well as getting the money. The minister, as I gathered from reading his speech, seems to have realized that taxes of this kind do destroy enterprises of this kind. I take it that the tax is temporary, and that it will be removed as soon as the drastic need for money is passed or some other and better and less destructive form of taxation can be adopted by virtue of public opinion at large and by public opinion in this house. Therefore I am hoping that this tax will disappear just as soon as the need for the money has gone by. I am not going to vote against this tax, much as I dislike it, because I realize-not that I am compelled at all-that it is necessary to support the administration in the measure which they have adopted, no doubt after considerable consideration, to raise the necessary money to carry on the war.
I want also to congratulate my fellow-member, the hon. member for Brantford City. If it were within the range of possibility, in view of the problems that he faces, for the Minister of Finance to ameliorate this tax, even in its temporary form, on the lower housing units, I am sure that it would be accepted by all members of this house with pleasure and satisfaction. I realize, however, the difficulty in so doing. It is a sales tax. It is not a specific tax, and you cannot make fish of one and flesh of the other without practical administrative difficulties.
There is this further point I wish to make in connection with the tax. A tariff tax obstructs the business of the country.

It does nothing of the
kind.
Why, of course it does.

I have seen a business
grow, under a tariff, from thirty-seven employees to 925.

Yes. You can grow
bananas in this country under those conditions. I am not going to debate -
