You cannot do any such
thing. You cannot grow bananas in this country.

I have been delighted with the type of argument addressed to a taxation measure which I have heard from the opposition, and I hope that if they ever take office they will remember the things they have said, which are contrary to the kind of debate that went on in years gone by.

What
about sugar?
The tax on sugar?
Yes.
Well, of course, I do not like that type of taxation.

But the
hon. member will vote for it.

I am going to vote for
it because I cannot help it.

Go back
to 1933 and see what your leader said about it.

He did not like it. Of
course he did not like it. We, no doubt, will abolish it as soon as the Minister of Finance can get money other ways.

Oh, yes!
They did not abolish it in 1935. There was no war on then.

No; but there was a
Tory opposition which no doubt supports that kind of taxation, not in its particular items, but in the main.
Let me finish the point so far as housing is concerned. A tariff tax, as I said, destroys the business of the country. Hon. members will find that that is so.
Your temporary deskmate, the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), does not agree with you.

Well, that is all right.
My hon. friend can make a tariff speech some day, and I will answer him with a free trade speech, or a freer trade speech. But we are not discussing that now.
What will be the result of this tax? In the first instance it will increase the cost of materials which go into a house; how much, I leave others to debate; but there will be an increase, and to that extent it will make the building of houses more difficult and costly.
There are two items which enter into costs of houses. First, there is the cost of the
land, and, second, there is the cost of the building. The building costs are determined by such items as these.

That is
deep stuff!

Taxes and so forth are
all added to the cost of the house. The cost of the land is what the owner can get. Is that not true?
Yes; this is deep stuff!

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has made many speeches to which I could refer with sarcasm, but I have never yet interrupted him, and I do not think a statement of that kind by him in this chamber is becoming.

I am
sorry.
All right. Then I withdraw what I said.
Carried.

Unanimously. The two costs are, first, the cost of the house and, then, the cost of the land. The cost of the land is what the owner can get for it. The increased cost of the buildings will for a while check building, but the final effect will be that the land-owner will take less for his land, and building will go on.
He is not getting much for his land new.
In my opinion he is getting too much.

I
know of lots which are sold for $^5.

The hon. member for Parkdale got nowhere with his building project. Why? I do not know whether he will agree with me in this statement, but practically every building project we ever had was ruined by the rapacity of the landlords.
My view is that municipal taxation had a great deal to do with it.
Yes, perhaps.
Very high municipal taxation.

Yes. There was too little on land values. What will happen is that, if this tax continues until adjustment takes place, there will be a decrease in the price which the owner of the lot can hold out for, and probably building will continue. That will apply, partly, if not wholly,- check for a while, a readjustment, and I hope building will continue. I also hope that in
Special War Revenue Act

due season the Minister of Finance will report that this tax has been removed, is out of the way.

I wish to say a word about this item before it passes. I believe it is necessary for the committee and the minister to bear in mind that we are concerned not only with raising money but with maintaining morale. There are at least three things which are necessary to the maintenance of morale. One of these, which already has been referred to several times, is health. Another is the cost of living. Yet another is the cost of production. This tax will affect disadvantageously our Canadian economy in all three of these respects.
I believe that it will be quite in order, and it may interest the committee, if I read a letter which I have received from the International Union of the United Automobile Workers of America, district council No. 26 of Ontario, dated May 20, sent from Wyandotte street, Windsor, Ontario. Long before we finish this war we shall have to take carefully into account the effect of our acts upon our labour unions and upon our working people generally. I shall leave out the address:
Dear Sir:
Attached is a copy of a resolution which was passed by District Council 26, UAWA-CIO, on March 30 and since adopted by all UAWA-CIO locals in Canada.
We respectfully ask that you give your utmost support to this resolution.
Yours truly,
John A. Taylor, Secretary pro tem.
To me that has an ominous significance. Here is the resolution:
Whereas: the rapid expansion of industry and the resultant demand for labour in the various industrial centres has caused an acute shortage in housing, and
Whereas: this shortage in housing is causing an overcrowded and unhealthy condition which will result in the development of disease and general epidemics, and
Whereas: this problem is an immediate one and if neglected may seriously hinder the war effort, and
Whereas: the dominion government is contemplating the spending of huge sums of money on projects such as the St. Lawrence, whose benefits will not be felt for years to come, and which government spending at this time will cause dissatisfaction among the people,
Be it therefore resolved:
That we, this District Council 26, of the United Automobile Workers of America, demand that the government immediately launch an ample and effective housing programme in order to adequately meet this serious crisis that is developing in housing.
May I, quite calmly, draw the minister's attention to the fact that the letter states

that that resolution has been passed by every local throughout Canada? May I also draw his attention, very sympathetically and firmly, to the fact that, not only is the government apparently taking no steps to institute a housing programme, but the minister is proposing a tax which will have the very opposite effect on housing conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, there is a housing programme. There is the war-time housing programme.
Would the minister say that this programme would offset the deleterious effects of this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not admit that the tax will have deleterious effects.

The minister has
established a reputation in this chamber for several characteristics during this debate, and now the characteristic of optimism comes out, I am afraid the minister is unduly optimistic about the tax. No further comment is necessary on the evil effects which this tax will have on people generally throughout the country, the poor people, those in the lower-income brackets, the sort of people who will save for two years in order to put on a front-door protection. I wonder how many members have been in that class, the class to whom it is a thrill just to put a verandah on a little shack. There are too many people in that class in Canada, and they are not looking with any degree of optimism upon the minister's proposal to impose this sales tax.
I wish to deal briefly now with the effect which the tax will have on the farming population. While I represent an urban population, I also represent, in the main, farmers. This year, I fancy, a great many bins will be necessary all over western Canada. Many people will grow wheat notwithstanding the desperate efforts of the government to reduce acreage. They will grow barley and oats, and they will require bins. The amount which will be added to the cost of farmers' bins by the discontinuance of this exemption is a matter that deserves careful consideration. The hon. member for Cumberland referred to the need for the reconstruction and repairing of barns. There is a great need for repairing barns throughout the west, wherever I have been. If farmers have not been able to do anything in the way of repairing buildings all through these wearisome and desolating depression years, now when they might be able to recoup their losses and make good the depreciation they are forbidden by taxation like this. How long will the farmers continue to have buildings

Special War Revenue Act
on their farms? I do not wish to labour this matter, but I do not want to point out that this little item will add to the costs of production for the farmer.
Before closing, I would refer to another matter which should affect the minister, and I believe it does. I have great respect for his application, intelligence, understanding, and all these fine qualities, but I wish to point out to him a fact which I have mentioned in debates at which he might not have been present, that the cost of living of the western farmer has increased since 1913, according to the Searle report, in these proportions. In 147 items which the western farmers buy, the cost has risen from 100 to 145; it was 100 in 1913-14, and it is 145 now. In so far as our farmers are carrying on and trying to live, they must buy these commodities and contrive to pay for them, and they must contrive to pay that 145 as against 100 which they paid in 1913-14. While they are endeavouring to do that, a gasoline tax is added; the sales tax is applied to lumber; they are discouraged from producing the quantity of wheat they ordinarily do, and they are unable to sell wheat for the cost of production. Hon. members need only put themselves in imagination in the position of the farmer and ask themselves whether it is wise, even for revenue, to apply this measure to the lumber which farmers buy. I protest against it.
Will the minister say whether the National Housing Act will be amended so as to raise the $2,500 to $3,000 and allow the 90 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not reply to the hon. member's suggestion because I did not realize from the manner in which he spoke that he expected an answer now. It was not because I did not appreciate the tone and spirit of the suggestion. I hesitate about making a speech on the whole situation for fear I shall start another round of speeches which might take all evening. I hesitate, but not because the government considers that it has no good reasons. It has good reasons. It is of opinion that most of the building which will be discouraged by the tax, if any volume of business is discouraged-and probably some will be- could far better take place in the immediate post-war period than now, when our object should be to devote our resources, material and human, more directly to the prosecution of the war than we should be doing by building homes and improving those that we have.
There may be instances where improvements are urgently needed, instances where the building of some homes is urgently required. With regard to the latter, the programme of the war-time housing corporation
takes care of the situation so far as the housing of workers for war-time industries is concerned. I am of opinion, however, that to permit this exemption to continue at a time like this would do more harm than good. The object of our governmental activities is not now primarily to improve the conditions under which our people live. Our peace-time thinking is likely to carry over into the period of war. Members of parliament would naturally like to see their constituents as comfortable and prosperous as possible, but I say again-and it may sound odd; it may sound as if we have not an adequate sense of responsibility

that the prosperity of our people, their material wellbeing, their comfort and convenience-perhaps I should leave our the word "convenience"- and so forth, is not the primary consideration at the present time. There should be no want or unemployment, but there should be none of that comfortable type of prosperity which is associated with a boom. I wish to make it perfectly clear that this is the policy of the government, whether or not that policy is attacked; I do not wish to make any bones about standing on that.
It was for these reasons, Mr. Chairman, we considered that this exemption should not be continued. It must be remembered that if building materials had not been removed from the list of taxable items, as they were in the spring of 1938, we never would have had this debate at all; it never would have occurred to any hon. member that they should have been removed at this time. Building materials were always taxable, even during the depression years of 1932, 1933, 1934, 1935 and 1936. It was not until 1938 that we took building materials out of that list, in order to meet the unemployment situation; and the reason for removing building materials from the list of taxable items has now disappeared. The hon. member for Saskatoon City says that there is some unemployment on the prairies, but generally speaking there is no unemployment situation in Canada to-day. As a matter of fact, Ontario members from rural constituencies have risen in their places one after another and asked if we realized how hard it is for farmers to get help on their farms. There are wide areas in Canada where the problem is not one of unemployment; the trouble is to get people to do the work. Under those circumstances we are not in favour of policies which will promote building that may very well run into excess building, which could far better be done in the period immediately after the war,
Those are the reasons for this policy. There will be some instances where somebody may desist from building when that building would
Special War Revenue Act

be a good thing, everything considered, but those instances will be only a very small percentage of the total number affected. It is impossible to frame taxes that will apply with precise equity in 100 per cent of the cases, but I am satisfied that this tax will substantially meet the requirements of the situation.
With regard to the question of the hon. member for Brantford City, unless the government is prepared to introduce an important amendment to the housing act this session- which I must say is not on the sessional programme-the limit will have to remain at $2,500, because that is statutory. It is a matter for consideration as to whether that limit should be increased, but I am afraid my answer to the hon. gentleman will have to be that it will not be increased this session.
With regard to the other suggestion-and I am sorry he has put me in the position of having to turn down his suggestions-that we exempt building materials from the tax in so far as they go into low-cost houses, I am advised that it would be impossible to trace the materials. The administrative difficulties would be so great that the suggestion could not be favourable considered.
Would the minister say just a word about repairs? I suggest that the tax on repairs was rather unfair, and might cause rents to be increased in some instances.

You could not follow the
materials into the repair jobs.

There is no doubt that the margin of rentals in certain places is so close at the present time that this tax may have some effect. At least it will provide an excuse for raising rents. When I was speaking about the Toronto Housing company I neglected to mention that for many year3 the shareholders of that company received no dividends at all. As a matter of fact, they have had hardly any return on their money.

When shall said bill be read the third time? Now?

No, Mr. Speaker. When this bill was in committee I was called to order by the chairman when I attempted to discuss the Bank of Canada and other matters. I do not wish to obstruct this bill, but I should like to know if there will be any opportunity to discuss the Bank of Canada in general and the foreign exchange control board in particular. Up to now it has been impossible to touch these people. When the matter is brought up in committee the chairman says we must adhere strictly to the rules. It is only under the shadow of the Chair-I mean the big one-that there is the real freedom of speech that I expect in this house. I do not wish to oppose the third reading of this bill, provided I have an opportunity some time to discuss these other matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On one of the finance estimates the hon. gentleman will be given an opportunity to discuss the operations of the foreign exchange control board, if that will be sufficient for his purposes.
And the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bank of Canada is not a government department; it is a separate organization, whose directors are nominated by the government. I should not like to give any undertaking about the Bank of Canada, except as far as the hon. gentleman can relate anything he would like to say about its operations to the discussion of the foreign exchange control board, which is an agency of the Department of Finance.
On the administration item under finance would there not be an opportunity to discuss any corporation or board controlled by the government? Surely there must be that opportunity somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will go as far as I can on the matter of the Bank of Canada, but I do not think I would agree to a discussion of the policies or internal administration of the Bank of Canada, because it is a separate organization.
Do I understand the minister to say that the Bank of Canada is not directly under the control of the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Correct.

Special War Revenue Act
That it is independent of the finance department, and therefore independent of this house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.
Independent of the administration, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what stage we are at, but the Bank of Canada is a separate organization, just like the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. These separate corporations are owned by the government; in the case of the Bank of Canada the stock is owned by the government and the directors are nominated by the government, but once the directors are appointed, I have no right, nor has the government any right, to dictate to the Bank of Canada as to what its policies shall be.

I distinctly dissent from that proposal, that in all these government-owned organizations parliament has lost control. That is distinctly not true in connection with the Canadian National Railways; and it must never be the accepted principle in this House of Commons or in this Canada of ours that any of these boards set up by the government as public agencies shall never be referred to in this house. I wish to register a protest against that statement of the minister.

Mr. Speaker, this is a good time to remind hon. members of certain views which have been expressed about taxation. There is across the boundary line a gentleman most favourably known over there; I am referring to the under-secretary of the treasury, Mr. Hanes of Washington.
I have in my hand the magazine section of the New York Times for April 9, 1939-over two years ago-and I find contained therein some of the views expressed by Mr. Hanes, a gentleman who had had practical experience before he attempted to apply his theories to the business of the country. This is what I find in the New York Times magazine:
There emanated from the treasury a series of suggestions, all with the Hanes stamp on them, to reduce the number of tax levies upon corporations in the interest of getting money to work;
to lay out a "five-year plan" of taxation so that business could know, for a time at least, what to expect;-
That is very important.
-and to eliminate all tax exemptions on future securities and salaries of federal, state and local governments.
Then it continues:
All the while Mr. Hanes continued to preach cooperation-between government and business, between industry ,and labour, even between labour and labour. "Our country is highly interrelated," he told this interviewer, "and we must all go up or down together. We must respect each other's ideas; even those we like least may sometimes give us a valuable idea if we grant the right to speak freely."
Note the -words "if we grant the right to speak freely." It continues:
"We don't want any suppressed or persecuted group in this country. For my own part one of. the things I work at hardest is my trusteeship in the Hampton institute for improving the lot of the negro,-"
I may point out that the Hanes family came from the south, and secured the help of negroes to establish their fortune. It continues:
"-and I realize that no matter how hard I work I can never repay more than a fraction of what the negroes' labour did in building up the Hanese in the south.''
Then Mr. Hanes is quoted as follows:
"Material, economic recovery," he said, "is the first problem in this democracy. In those parts of the world where democracy has been forced to give way to one-man government, it has come about when the economic condition of the people was unbearable."
Let us not forget that.
"One of the most important economic movements to-day is remedial federal taxation that will make for recovery."
Then the article continues:
What of Mr. Hanes's philosophy of taxation? Would he say that he was against using taxes to effect reforms, and for regarding taxes solely as a means of getting money to run thj government? The question, he found, was hard to 'answer in that form.
"The matter of ability to pay is fundamental to our tax system," he said. "We have to start with -that. Then we have to admit that all taxes, of any sort, have social repercussions upon our economy and on individuals. But I do not believe in setting out to write a tax bill to do by indirection what you dare not do by direction."
That is very aptly put.
"The motive for any tax, whether for reform or anything else, should be made clear to congress, which will then be in a position to accept or reject. In a democracy the people are trusting their public servants and should not be deceived."
That is another very good thing.
"I believe," he said, "that the treasury will collect a larger total of tax dollars with a tax
Special War Revenue Act

bill that takes into broad consideration the effect of the dollars it will leave the taxpayer for expansion and development than it will by concentrating on the highest possible dollar it can extract from the business, profession or occupation of the taxpayer."
Mark you, sir.
"In other words, what is left to the taxpayer is as important to the country's economy as what is taken from him.
"The point is that, in my judgment, harsh or deterrent tax laws do not produce the maximum flow of revenue. I firmly believe that the one way to lighten the load of to-morrow is to adjust in fairness the load of to-day."
That is one of the wisest presentations on taxation I have seen. Of course someone will tell me that that was written a few months before the war.
All right; let me now quote from a Canadian publication known as Canadian Business. In the April, 1940, issue of this publication I find a worth-while article written by no less a person than Mr. C. Fraser Elliott, K.C.,. income tax commissioner for Canada. The article has been summarized in a frame in the middle of the page. This summary is contained in a few brief sentences, and is headed "Highlights". I assume every hon. member has seen the article, because the magazine has been sent to us free of charge, and it is worth reading. The boxed-in portion of the article is as follows:
Highlights
Tax Administrator and taxpayer have a common interest in:
1.	The minimizing of taxation's detrimental effects.
2.	A simplicity in tax laws.
3.	The encouragement of profits.
4.	An absence of wilful evasion.
5.	The minimizing of administrative difficulties.	_	_
6.	An avoidance of tax discrimination.
7.	A cooperative effort to finance the war efficiently.
That is concise and also sensible. The difference is mainly in phraseology; the meaning of what Mr. Hanes and Mr. Elliott said on two different occasions is about the same. As I say, about the only difference is in the expression. One was written before the war; the other, several months after the war had started. It is written by a Canadian who is more familiar with our problems than the average citizen. In February last, no less a man than Mr. P. D. Houston, president of the American bankers' association and chairman of the American National bank of Nashville, Tennessee, made an important statement at a convention which took place in Chicago on February 12. I have the reports of the New York Herald-Tribune and the New York Times of February 13. Of course his remarks apply to the United States, but I should like to quote this report as follows:

Banking aid urged in defence orders.
Government credit now will lead to dependence later, P. D. Houston declares.
Business challenge seen.
Any failures will be blamed on trade by "alibi boys" head of the A.B.A. says.
We have a lot of alibi boards. I wonder what is the responsibility of these men in the United States? Here they are irresponsible. It is impossible to say anything about them. May I read a letter which I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in connection with the matter of free speech in the house. It is to be found on page 4599 of Hansard of May 26, 1939, and I am asking that it be placed again on Hansard. I think it should be placed on Hansard at every session in order that we may have free speech in this house. It reads:
My dear Chief:
Referring to vour remarks at page 1862 of Hansard of March 14, you stated that you did feel that, as leader of the House of Commons, it was part of your duty to see that members of the public service "who are not in a position to speak for themselves during the course of debates which take place in this house, should be protected against any remarks in the nature of a reflection upon themselves".
The suggestion that the wrongdoings of public servants cannot be discussed in the house was at first an invention of the Ottawa papers which cater to the public service and it was brought to the house in the first place by the members of the C.C.F. party to prevent any exposure of their own friends in the service.
I submit respectfully that according to British parliamentary practice, every civil servant is represented in the house by the head of his department. Therefore, as you stated that you were the last person in the house who would wish to curtail in any way my freedom of discussion, I have the unquestionable right of expressing my opinion about any civil servant who cannot sit in the house and be present there because he receives an emolument from the crown. The minister is there to take cognizance of and answer any complaint made by any member of parliament. If the minister is familiar with the matter, he may answer at once; if not, he shall take note of what has been said and give an answer in due course.
Some ministers assume that they always have to take the side of all civil servants in their departments, even when some things have been done against their own instructions or outside of their own knowledge. It seems all wrong because it is an incitement to civil servants to do worse, as they can rely upon their minister's continuous defence to consider themselves unimpeachable, except perhaps when they have been found guilty of a criminal offence.
You went further in objecting to the "references to their personal history such as the hon. member I gather was about to make".
It is pretty hard on a member to object on a guess on what he is going to say. For your information, I must tell you that what I intended to show was the record of experience of the deputy minister of finance, to which your predecessor had vaguely referred but which he. himself, had conspicuously hidden._ I agree with you that "members of the public service

Special War Revenue Act
have to look to the administration for protection in the discharge of their duties", but on the other hand, it is the duty of members of parliament to inform the government on everything they find wrong in the civil service, in order to secure a possible improvement.
For the above-mentioned reasons, I regret to have to disagree with your statement that "if deputy ministers or leading public officials or any members of the public service are to be attacked here, in justice to them they should have the right to make reply on their own behalf from wherever they may happen to be".
They are entitled to no right of reply to what is said by members of parliament, but it is the duty of the minister concerned to reply, in his capacity as head of the department.
Again for the above-mentioned reasons, if the method which you have suggested "were to be adopted with regard to the conduct of our public affairs I am afraid the public service of the country could not be carried on in the manner in which the country has a right to expect it will be carried on". I want you to understand clearly that I did not intend to bring "personal matters" in the debate; my intention was solely to tell the house about the record of experience of a man who is mainly responsible for the blind and bold dictatorship of the finance department in dominion government.
Standing order No. 41, speaks for itself:
"No member shall speak disrespectfully of his majesty, nor of any of the royal family; nor of the governor or person administering the government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof."
It makes no mention of anyone in the civil service.
My intention was not at all to attack you nor your colleague of the finance department, but to inform both of you on matters of public interest which are purposely kept in the dark by those concerned.
The first duty of a member of parliament is to inform the government on what he considers of public importance, and it is only after he has done so that he may be justified in attacking the ministers concerned, in case no action is taken to redress the wrong which was complained of.
I would not feel myself "justified" of "attacking" any cabinet minister for anything done outside of his knowledge by anyone in his department, unless such minister were previously informed about the facts and where is it to be done elsewhere than in the house?
Then you said I was "quite within (my) his rights in bringing to the house anything at all in connection with the attitude of individual civil servants", etc.
The competence and qualification of any civil servant are even more important than his attitude and how can they be rated if their record of experience is to be left outside the picture?
I am just reading the -wonderful biography of your illustrious grandfather who was a champion of free speech and I hope that all the sacrifices that he made during his lifetime for the freedom of speech in the legislative assembly were not made in vain and that we have not regressed a century backwards, to the time of the "family compact". Otherwise, it would be just as well to suppress parliament.
Faithfully yours,
Tean Frangois Pouliot.
What I find strange is that instead of giving us the information about Canadian affairs for which we have been asking so long, the Bank of Canada gave us information about German finance, described the way in which Germany was financing the war and pictured Hitler as a great financial hero. It seems to me that, as this war proceeds, our main business is to know how much the Canadian citizen can pay in the prosecution of the war, what taxes are being collected from him and what taxes can be collected with a view to creating the least possible disturbance in finance. Those are my humble views about taxation, and I hope, sir, that I shall not be considered too hard when I say that I find Mr. Towers' dissertation on German finance in the annual report of the Bank of Canada both uncalled for and ridiculous at this time. I am not going to read it here; I have no time to waste. I will just draw the attention of my hon. colleagues in this house to the fact that it can be found in the Canada Gazette of February 13, 1941.
Exactly two years after the interview with Mr. Hanes, published in the New York Times, an interesting article appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of April 9, 1941. The heading on the article reads, "Pictures Canada as richer after war-Poorer too, greater resources, skill, fewer material things, Professor predicts

Saddled with debt." The article reads:
In the aggregate Canada will be richer after the war than she ever has been before, Professor J. McCurdy of the department of philosophy at the university of Toronto told members of the So-Ed club of the Central Y.M.C.A. last night.
"Canada will have greater resources and vastly more still both among trained workers and leaders in statesmen, in administering a bigger business in social ownership," he declared, "but distributively Canada will be poorer. There will be more cash in the pockets of the workers and less in those of the middle class and salaried workers. We will be poorer in material things-fewer new roofs on houses, fewer replaced cars and clothing that we wear longer."
It is precisely the middle class which is contributing its money in taxation to finance the war. Everybody is ready to contribute his share of taxes, provided that the money is well spent and provided that accounts are furnished to the people. It is to my great surprise that the accounts are incomplete. There are, of course, no regular estimates for the war departments; as was pointed out earlier in the session, the reports of the auditor general are incomplete, and therefore it is impossible to get information on -where the money goes. "It is a war secret", and so on. These fellows are there, and it is impossible for members of parliament to check them and to give fruitful advice to the minister
Special War Revenue Act

although we are always willing to do so. They make it impossible for us to cooperate with the minister, and what are they? They are pictured as angels; they are pictured as saints; they are pictured as experts, and they are pictured as the only saints and the only experts in this country. We have to listen to them. We are willing to help, but we cannot help because of that.
Yesterday I took the trouble to go home, covering a distance of 800 miles, just to speak in favour of the victory loan and to encourage my people to subscribe to it. On the other hand, I said to them, "I am suggesting that you subscribe to the victory loan, but when I get back to Ottawa I assure you that I will scrutinize all expenditures even more closely than I ever did before. I will scrutinize them with a magnifying glass. I have urged you to subscribe to the victory loan, and you are entitled to full information as to how the money is being spent." There is no possible reason why this information should be refused to members of parliament, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was absolutely right in what he said just before the recess. There is no possible reason why anybody who is employed and paid by the government should hide any kind of expenditure, and there is not a single Canadian citizen outside this house who would ever submit the contrary. The suggestion would be absurd.
On the very same day, April 9, 1941, the Toronto Daily Star had another article headed, "Supply Department soon to spend $5,000,000 daily.	Has	placed	total	of
81,500,000,000 in war orders in year's operations. Birthday review." But again no information.
I told my electors at home yesterday that I was in favour of the victory loan but, on the other hand, that the best way to get large subscriptions to the loan was to give members of parliament the information for which they asked. Hide nothing. Put all the cards on the table. That is what I am asking on behalf of my people, and I am sure that that can be said for every constituency. I have the utmost respect for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I have told him repeatedly that I have confidence in him, but I have lost confidence in the experts placed round him because they have been placed there by a man who was supposed to have converted John Strachey and Trebistch Lincoln. The former was considered so crazy that he was deported from the United States. Even with a letter of recommendation from R. B., the latter was again deported from England. It is that man who has shown such good judgment in the selection of his

good friends, Trebistch Lincoln and Strachey, who infested the civil service with cranks who are still there and who are a curse to the country. I may be considered sacrilegious for saying this. It is time for us to wake up. It is time for us to do what William Lyon Mackenzie did, and fight for responsible government. I sometimes hear some ministers say "We have assumed a great responsibility." It is no ministerial responsibility at all. It is done as a matter of course. They are there in those posts, and they have to take action. That' is not ministerial responsibility. Ministerial responsibility is the rendering of accounts for every cent that comes from the taxpayers' pockets. Everyone knows that is ministerial responsibility.
One other thing. It is even suggested that in time of war we should not discuss in the House of Commons or in committee matters of sentiment, that we should have the kind of speech that Isaac delivered when he was going to be burned as a sacrifice. Isaac was there ready to be cremated, offering himself as a sacrifice. It should not be that at all here. In the House of Commons we must have the spirit of fighters, the same spirit as the soldiers have on tlje battlefield, not that of prisoners of war in a concentration camp. That is my humble view. Moreover, instead of considering matters from the point of view of sentimentalism, we should be able to reason about them. To do that, we must have information, and no one can deny us information which is due to us. Of course, sometimes hairs are split very fine. What is said to us is not a lie; it is not a distortion of the truth; it is not even a fib; it is a kind of juggling with the facts. Information given to us must be plain, complete and accurate, and the accounts given us must be such as we can understand. That has not always been the position here. I have had to teach some of the officials of the service how to do their work; it rvas much the same as teaching a professor how to spell. I say again that there are numbers of people who think they can read and write and who do not know even their alphabet, but so long as they wear a mortarboard they are experts and geniuses.
Here is another clipping from the same paper, the Toronto Star of April 9, 1941:
Credit account may be set up to aid Canada..
Forecast King, Roosevelt, to plan closer cooperation between nations. Lease munitions?
This is interesting. We are on good terms with the neighbouring republic, and that fact may mean a great deal to us. The committee may remember that the member for Temis-couata was one of the first to advocate an alliance with the United States. The Prime

Special War Revenue Act
Minister told him that it was not the time to speak of that; that it was dangerous; that he was hurting the whole show by suggesting that he was in favour of an alliance. Then, I remember, my friend the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulfordt) also spoke of it the same day in August of last year. We did that because we consider that, when we have a powerful neighbour next to us, we must be on good terms with him. Occasionally we need his help, and we must have it. But that does not mean that we must copy from him all that is bad; we must copy from him only what is good.
My last remark is that we should not consider taxation as though the war were being lost. We are all determined to win the war, but taxation must be related to our needs. At the present time taxation is just the same as though the deluge were coming to-morrow -"after us, the deluge." Taxation should be clear, progressive, and in accordance with the means of the people.
Not only that; the policy which has been preached by Messrs. Towers et al., the policy of restriction and curtailment, is a policy of misery. Everyone knows that the prosperity of a nation is not shown only by the bank accounts; they are only part of the picture. National prosperity is indicated in the clearings of the banks, meaning that the nation is richer because there are more sales, and then it is easier to collect from savings. This is the reason why so many important data are collected by the bureau of statistics with regard to bank clearings. They show the course of the dollar which goes from pocket to pocket, enriching everyone and permitting everyone to pay more taxes. That is opposed to the policy of curtailment and of restriction, which has been preached by the Towers' group. He is the highest paid civil servant in Canada and one of the highest paid in America; he receives 830,000 a year, and Iris advice is, "Don't spend. Tighten your belts." Where shall we be headed for if that policy is adopted? What will happen is that the government will have a great deal of difficulty in collecting enough taxes to meet its requirements.
Therefore I am always ready to cooperate with the minister, provided that I am not regarded as a country cousin. I represent a rural seat; but I contend that any member of parliament, even the humblest, he who represents the district farthest from Ottawa, is better qualified to offer suggestions to the Minister of Finance than any one of these men. I have not mentioned them all; I have not time to do so. But if a man comes here with a Ph.D. honoris causa, he is deemed qualified to give advice to the Minister of Finance,
and his erratic views become government policy. Have I to subscribe to it and support it as the government's programme? Well, well!
I want the war to be conducted upon an effective basis. I want my people to suffer the least possible during the war, and I want this government to keep power, but I want also to get rid at once of all the asses that have been put in high places by R. B. Bennett.

I wish for just four or five minutes to discuss the third reading of the bill. I am sorry that, since, I had to leave at four o'clock on Friday, I was not here when it came up in the committee stage.
I believe that it is a mistake for the government to adopt the principle set out in part XV of the bill, namely, that the governor in council shall have power to make rules and regulations regarding amusements, leaving the whole problem in mystery and doubt, and in politics. So far as this problem is concerned, the third day after the war broke out I urged upon the house and upon the government that the government should declare a national policy for amusements and sports in Canada, that they should have a survey made of all amusements, amateur sports and professional sports in the country and in relation to the war, lay down a principle or a coherent policy with respect to sports and amusements and whether everything should be as usual in Canada. Like the British, we are a sport-loving people.
Sports are of two kinds, professional and amateur. The Canadian intercollegiate union suspended all their schedules, not only of football but as regards hockey, track, soccer, boxing, basketball and other sports, for the whole period of the war. In so doing they followed the principle which the college union adopted in the great war. Also the Big Four in rugby suspended operations in the great war, not in this. I am not here to say anything on that matter. What I am suggesting is that the government would be well-advised to have a survey for ne^t year made showing what sports are being carried on, the number of those participating who have undertaken the thirty-day and four-month programmes of training, the number who have enlisted, and the contribution of each branch to our war effort. Sports' funds have done a great deal in this war for the cause.
As regards amateur sports, and particularly regarding the Big Four of rugby, I have here a letter from the president of the Argonaut rowing club, a splendid soldier, citizen and
Special War Revenue Act

amateur sportsman, Major T. H. C. Alison. He was president of Royal Henley and the Big Four in rugby.
As you know, being a past president of the Argonaut club, we depend solely on football to keep the club going. We never make a profit, and always have a deficit. In fact our overdraft at the bank right now is close to $2,000.
Next year the club celebrates its seventieth anniversary and we may be closed up if we caunot keep football going.
I think you will agree that we have done a lot for amateur sport in Canada.
Lord Strathcona once said that an Argonaut crew in England did more for Canada than all the immigration agents there.
We had a crew in England in 1939 when they celebrated their hundredth anniversary at Henley.
That is just one amateur club. Other rowing clubs in Toronto district have been closed up, the Dons, Varsity and others; they cannot make things go, owing to the depression, the war and one thing or another. The canoe clubs are in the same position. The harbour commissioners had a program of rebuilding the port; one half was a beautification and amusement schemes, and the other half an industrial scheme.
In the early days of our city the late Edward Hanlan went all over the world and did a great deal to advertise the city, while champion oarsman of the world. The winning of the war is Canada's first, last and only ousiness; nothing else counts. Consider that in this question.
In my opinion a national survey should be made along that line so that the government might be able to gather information for submission to parliament at the next session. So far as baseball and a number of other sports are concerned, they have been in the red for many years. The Toronto baseball club did a lot for the city and that sport, and many public-spirited men-the late Lawrence Solman, for instance-who have been associated with these sports and have done a good deal to promote them in the interests of the Canadian people, have never made anything out of them. This is true of amateur hockey and other sports. I suggest that the government has gone too far in imposing a tax of 20 per cent to start with. True, some amendments are in the act. They might have reduced it to 10 per cent or even to 5 per cent for amateur contests and smaller amusements, and made it applicable to all theatres and professional sports without discrimination, but I do not think it is at all fair as it stands. The amateurs should not pay. I might mention, incidentally, with reference to the interest taken in amateur sports, the Canadian secondary schools' splendid regatta in Toronto in

which several high schools and six collegiate institutes participated. No gates were taken. It was all free and a wonderful sight. These high school young people are doing their part in the war, both in connection with munitions and in the work they do on the farms to secure a matriculation, and they should have some recognition. Take the Argonauts in Toronto. They have to supply oars, boats, and everything else to teach these high school youths, and they make nothing. There are no gates in aquatic sports like canoeing and rowing. There are no paid managers in these clubs. There is a paid trainer and sometimes a coach in football, but there are no paid managers.
I agree with leader of the opposition in what he has said with regard to amateur sports, but so far as professional hockey is concerned, I think the government has gone, in the rate in the bill, much too far. A large number of public-spirited business men in Toronto built the magnificent Maple Leaf Gardens in that city, where meetings can be held three hundred and sixty-five days in the year. They did a great work for Toronto, and never got a nickel out of it. It is unquestionably a great asset not only to the city of Toronto but to the country generally, and those associated with this patriotic sporting enterprise have done a great deal to promote the welfare of various classes in connection with sports and community work as has their manager of the arena. I suggest that the government would be well advised to study the whole question more closely, by a national survey, and bring down a workable amendment next year with a study of the enlistments from each sport.
I am surprised that the bill did not contain a clause for the taxing of grain pools. There is a legal question involved in that connection, and in my opinion the day is not far distant when we shall have to follow the British example and tax all cooperative grain agencies and middlemen who handle grain. We shall have to do this as a means of raising revenue for the country in view of the large amount of money which the government spends in administering the grain act.
There should be give and take so far as amusements are concerned. I know some of the professional hockey men who went to the thirty-day camp, and they have said that they are willing to be called up if, as and when required, for further military service, but they have not yet been called. Again, 1 suggest it would be well to have a survey of this whole question with a view to adopting a national policy from coast to coast, so that everyone would do his part, and that we would

Income War Tax Act
cease to have everything as usual in Canada. The trouble in this country is, everything as usual so far, and our war effort is lagging. We do not know what is going on. We do not know who is going to own the country by the end of the year. The government should lay down a national policy as the Canadian universities have done. Amateur sports, with one or two exceptions, have not made any money. The various boards of education contests for various sports should continue for the war period. I hope the minister next year will bring down a measure which will be more equitable, fair and just to all concerned and be a safeguard for sports for sport's sake.
I object to this legislation being made a political football, giving the governor in council power to discriminate between one part of Canada and another, and so make rules. The governor in council may exempt one sport in the west, say in Winnipeg, and another down east. This simply drags the whole thing into politics. There should be a clear-cut definition so that we could know those who would be exempt and those who would not, and identify each sport. Leaving it to the governor in council is another matter of politics. So far as my experience goes, to leave such matters to rules and regulations of the governor in council is to open the door to politics, undesirable influence and sectional treatment, and that should not be allowed in sport.
Motion (Mr. Usley) agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 87, to amend the Income War Tax Act.
He said: There are a few remarks I should like to make on the second reading of the bill. There are two sections, 16 and 17, which I propose to ask to have stand until to-morrow. They are the sections relating to the nonresident tax, the proposal being to raise that tax from five to fifteen per cent. I do that because this matter is the subject of some correspondence by telegram between the Prime Minister and the Premier of Ontario, which I believe is not completed. There is one point about this correspondence which I should like to make clear but which apparently is not clear to the public and probably to the house. At least, some of the newspapers seem to have entirely misapprehended it. The telegrams were placed on the table. They included, dated May 28, one from the Premier of Ontario to the Prime Minister. It has been
assumed by some persons that this government attempted to link two matters together, namely, the acceptance of the dominion-provincial offer and the non-resident tax, and I believe this government has been attacked for so doing.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By certain sections of the , press. In order to make the matter clear, I wish to read to the house two paragraphs from a long telegram from the Premier of Ontario to the Prime Minister. It is the telegram to which I have referred, that of May 28. After objecting very strongly to the proposal to raise the non-resident tax on interest on provincial bonds from 5 to 15 per cent, Mr. Hepburn went on to say:
Now that you have made it abundantly clear to Ontario that you are determined not to remove the injustice against which Ontario and others have lodged emphatic protests, but that you propose to persevere in an action which is clearly designed to degrade the credit of the Canadian provinces, I deem it my duty to inform you that this your latest irritating act against the good relations which should exist between the dominion and provincial governments leaves the Ontario government no alternative but to advise you that it has decided to keep in its own hands the means whereby the services necessary to the well being of the citizens may be maintained at the highest state of efficiency. In no other way does the government of Ontario believe that its revenues and credit may be kept on the present levels, and you have given this province the very best reasons in the world for retaining full control and management of its own fiscal machinery.
In that paragraph the Premier of Ontario used the dominion proposal to increase the non-resident tax from 5 to 15 per cent as the reason why the government of Ontario felt that it could not accept the offer which the dominion government made to the provinces. That was a serious decision for the government of Ontario to make, and the ground upon which it made it, as stated in this telegram, seemed in many respects disproportionate to the seriousness of the decision; at least that was the view taken by this government.
Mr. Hepburn then went on to say:
You are hereby assured that this government, which has and is giving fullest cooperation in all matters pertaining to the prosecution of the war, will continue to cooperate with a view to bringing about what is most urgently required, namely, a full-out war effort to save Christian civilization.
Upon consideration of that position taken by the Ontario government, the reason given by the Ontario government for not accepting the dominion-provincial offer, which of course would have a most serious effect upon taxpayers, both corporate and individual, in this province, this government felt that it should
Income War Tax Act

avail itself of Mr. Hepburn's offer in the second paragraph to which I have referred, namely, to cooperate, and therefore the Prime Minister sent Mr. Hepburn this telegram, dated May 30.
Was it tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; this telegram has not yet been tabled. I wish to read it to the house:
Honourable Mitchell F. Hepburn,
Premier of Ontario,
Toronto, Ontario.
Referring to your telegram of May twenty-eighth my colleagues and I learn with keen regret of the attitude which you continue to take in regard to the increase of the tax on certain interest going to non-resident bondholders and that as a result of the imposition of this increased tax the government of Ontario has no alternative but to reject the offer made by the dominion to the provinces in the dominion budget of April twenty-ninth. I shall refrain from making any comments on your personal references or your observations with regard to other provincial governments and I shall not repeat the arguments advanced in my last telegram in regard to the proposed increase of the tax on non-residents. It is sufficient perhaps to say that after again reviewing the whole matter we are as strongly as ever of the opinion that this tax measure is a fair and reasonable one; that it involves only an increase in a tax which has been in effect since nineteen thirty-three without protest from the province of Ontario; that the proposed rate of tax is low as compared not only with taxes imposed on other income earned in Canada but also with similar taxes on income going to nonresidents imposed by countries of which our foreign bondholders are citizens; that it constitutes no threat to the credit of Ontario or of any other province, and that the tax is validly imposed and can be enforced. While we strongly hold this view nevertheless we are equally convinced that it would be most unfortunate were there to be any serious controversy between the dominion and the largest and wealthiest province of Canada at a time when the major consideration of all Canadians should be the most effective and most united prosecution of the war. Furthermore it is a matter of particular regret to us that under such conditions the government of Ontario should feel it necessary to regard the increase in this tax on foreign bondholders as a reason for refusing to accept the offer made to the provinces in the dominion budget. Were the matter to be left in this position, the citizens of Ontario would be prevented by prospective double taxation of their incomes from making as large subscriptions to the victory loan, to be offered on Monday next, as otherwise they would be able and willing to make. In view of these considerations and in order as quickly as possible to clarify the situation we would be willing to restore to its previous level the tax on provincial obligations held by foreign bondholders provided the government of Ontario on its part would be prepared to give the dominion prompt assurance of its willingness to accept the offer made to the provinces in the dominion budget.
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Was there an answer to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been no answer to that telegram.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); There was something in the press about the eat being out of the bag.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; the Premier of Ontario, ' on receipt of that telegram, is reported to have made some observation about the cat being out of the bag or something of that sort, and saying that he would lay the whole question before his government. If he has done so, no word of his decision has been received, and it is for that reason that if we reach those two sections, 16 and 17, to-night, I am going to ask the house to let them stand.
The main purpose I had in speaking as I am doing on the second reading of this bill was to make it perfectly clear that the two subjects were not linked together, not connected by us in the first instance with what the Premier of Ontario gave as his reason for not being able to accept the offer which the dominion made to all the provinces, namely, the raising of this non-resident tax from 5 to 15 per cent. While, as the Prime Minister said in the telegram, the government is of the opinion that the increase was quite justified, it did not feel that it should allow that matter, not as important in magnitude as the other, to stand in the way of the acceptance of that offer, so we telegraphed the Premier of Ontario, stating that if the withdrawal of that provision, putting the tax back to 5 per cent, would enable them to accept that offer, we would take that stand. It was not an attempt by us to use this as a way of forcing or hammering the province of Ontario into doing something we wanted them to do, but it was an endeavour on our part in that conciliatory way of accepting the offer of cooperation which is contained in the telegram of the Premier of Ontario, to meet him on his own ground and do what he said in order to remove the ground advanced by him for the province of Ontario not accepting this offer.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not rise for the purpose of discussing the matter immediately under review by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). To do so would not in my view serve a useful purpose at this time when the nation is appealing for the largest sum of money in its history'. I have read the correspondence with a great deal of interest, all except the last telegram which the minister has now placed

Income War Tax Act
upon the record and which was not available in the return that was brought down in the house a few days ago. I am of opinion that- and I say this after a great deal of consideration and after having tried to think the matter through in all its implications-if I were to-night, at this opportunity presented by the the Minister of Finance to take either side- to make an attack upon the Premier of Ontario for the attitude which he has taken, or, conversely, to make an attack upon the government of Canada for the attitude which it has taken-I should, I think, be justly accused of playing politics as between these two branches of the Liberal party, and of doing a distinct disservice to my country at a time when, of all times in the immediate period of our history, we should have the best exhibition of national unity that it is possible for us to have.
I have a view on this question with respect to the 15 per cent tax, but it is irrespective of the views attributed to the Minister of Finance or the Premier of Ontario. In my view it would be better if the government did not proceed with this provision. I do not, however, advance that view because of anything that has been said in this correspondence. I think I can safely leave this question, occupying the position which I do at this moment at ail events, on the ground that I have mentioned, namely, that to stir up a controversy or to provide an issue of, shall I say, provincial rights, at a time when our war situation is growing more critical from day to day and when the need of success for this great national loan is so great, or to throw in a spark of dissension that might kindle a flame, which, as between Ontario and the dominion, would sever this country, and would split public opinion wide open, would, in my opinion, be absolutely wrong, and I do not intend to do so.
I would rather suggest to the minister and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that the view expressed by the leader of the opposition in the Ontario legislature was a most constructive one. It was suggested that the Prime Minister of Canada should ask the premiers of the provinces to come together to see if, by round-table conference, an accommodation could not be arranged among the provinces with respect to, first, the whole question of the vacation of the field of income and corporation tax, and, second, the question of the taxation of provincial bond issues. That was a constructive suggestion, and I commend it to the Minister of Finance and to the Prime Minister, believing that it is not yet too late for them to take action. Perhaps I should treat this whole matter as a family row between members of the Liberal party, 14873-214
and drop it at that. It is not fitting to have this squabble going on at the present time, and I suggest that the only way to end it is by a conference round a table. That position I commend to all interested parties.
Having said that, I intend to proceed to another phase of the matter immediately tinder discussion. When the bill was in the committee stage, I adverted to a matter which I considered of considerable importance. It will be recalled that in his budget speech, on April 29, the minister, as reported at page 2345 of Hansard, made a statement and an announcement concerning proposals with respect to the vacation by the provinces of the income and corporation tax fields. At the risk of wearying hon. members for a few moments-and only for a few moments-I intend to cover that ground, and ask the minister for a declaration as to the position of the government with respect to only two aspects of the matter. I quote from the minister's speech:
After the most careful consideration of all the questions involved we have reached the conclusion that the rates of personal and corporation incomes taxes should be raised by the dominion to the maximum levels which would be reasonable at this time, if the provinces were not in those fields. Our plans are drawn, therefore, on that basis, and in due course I shall outline proposals to increase the minimum rates of corporation income tax to 40 per cent; to increase the rates of personal income taxes very considerably and to increase the national defence tax.
But these increases if taken together with the existing provincial rates would result in too heavy a burden and it is proposed, therefore, as a temporary expedient for the duration of the war only, to ask the provinces to vacate these two tax fields.
I am writing to the provincial premiers informing them that the dominion will offer to pay each year for the duration of the war, to any province which, together with its municipalities, will temporarily vacate the personal income tax and corporation tax fields either.
(a)	The revenues which the province and its municipalities actually obtained from these sources during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31, 1940, or
(b)	The cost of the net debt service actually paid by the province during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31, 1940 (not including contributions to sinking funds), less the revenue obtained from succession duties during that period.
Such payments will be augmented by appropriate fiscal-need subsidies where it can be shown that these are necessary. At the same time, it is proposed to discontinue the present special grants which are voted annually by parliament.
I pause at this juncture to point out that in making that statement the Minister of Finance realized, as we all do, that if an accommodation is not reached between the provinces on the one hand and the dominion on the other, those citizens of the provinces

Income War Tax Act

which are in the income tax field, and those corporations which are paying corporation taxes, will be compelled to bear a considerably increased and very heavy taxation. That is not a desirable thing.
Let me point out that there are at least two provinces which have no income tax. The citizens of Ontario will be obliged to bear-an additional burden and an additional load over and above what the citizens of Nova Scotia will bear. For that reason I urge the minister to come to some arrangement with the Premier of Ontario, if it is humanly possible to do so, in order that this discrimination against the citizens of this great province may not occur.
The Minister of Finance then went on to say:
The plan which I have outlined for alleviating [DOT]the present difficulties is by no means perfect and is not intended to be more than a temporary war-time expedient. However, it has the merits of simplicity. It will permit the dominion government to levy the necessary taxes without injustice to residents of different sections of the country or to different income groups.
That is exactly the position to which I have just referred. The minister continued:
As far as the provinces are concerned, it will ensure them a fixed revenue for each year during which the war continues, based upon the level of such revenues during the past year. In other words, the dominion guarantees the provinces an annual payment equivalent in all probability to the maximum amount which they have ever received from the two tax fields under discussion. It is true that if incomes continue to rise the provinces might receive even larger revenues from these two sources in the future than they did in the year 1940, but this would depend in part upon the course and nature of the war, in part upon the level and nature of dominion taxation and upon many other questions which cannot be foreseen or assessed at this time.
Then, this further brief extract from the same speech:
The alternative offer of the dominion to pay the cost of a province's debt service is intended for those provinces which have not developed to the same extent, the personal income tax and corporation tax fields and for those provinces which represent that they must be given some measure of relief pending a final solution of their present difficulties.
In the remarks I made on the budget I referred to these two proposals. It was my view then and it is my view now that the proposals were generous to the provinces, whichever alternative they desired to accept. I still am of that view, and I am still hopeful that the provinces, one and all, will accept. I understand that the smaller provinces are exploring the position, and that they are making their calculations. I had hoped that arrangements would have been concluded before this.

With respect, however, to certain provinces there is apt to be difficulty. I shall not refer again to the correspondence with the Premier of Ontario except to say that apparently at one stage he closed the door. In the oase of another province, Alberta, the premier has intimated, if one is to believe press reports, that he has adopted an attitude of watchful waiting, that he intends to see what the other provinces will do. I reaffirm and reiterate the opinion which I hold, that with respect to the great province of Ontario, no stone should be left unturned to get an accommodation, even though this government has to retrace its steps with respect to the 15 per cent tax. I think I should leave that position right there. I am expressing the hope that an arrangeement will be made. I do hope that an accommodation can be reached by meeting and discussing round the conference table the position that each jurisdiction has assumed. It can be done if there is the will to do. Knowing the Prime Minister as I do, I appeal to him to take the initiative in starting these discussions; otherwise the taxpayers of Ontario will suffer; an issue will be created, and there will be disunity in this country.
An entirely different situation exists with respect to Alberta. As I appreciate the situation, Alberta is not one of those provinces which have developed the personal income and corporation tax to a great degree. I may be wrong in that assumption, but that is the hypothesis upon which my remarks will be based. It is probable that in normal circumstances that province, assuming that it comes into the scheme, would accept alternative B, although it is only fair to say that so far as is known that province has not committed itself to the principle of either proposal. As I stated a moment ago, if newspaper reports are to be considered as accurately representing the position, Alberta has adopted a policy of watchful waiting to see * what other provinces will do. Be that as it may, however, if it adopts alternative B, then I put this question to the government: What is to be the attitude of this government with regard to that province, having regard to the fact that for several years the government of Alberta has repudiated its solemn obligation to pay in full the interest upon its bonds, much to the loss of its credit and also potentially affecting the credit of other provinces? Is this government, in dealing with Alberta, to pay only to that province the actual amount of bond interest paid by that province and thus recognize its default and thereby in effect condone its action? Or will it insist upon an arrangement being made by that province whereby the Alberta govern-

Income War Tax Act
ment will respect its responsibilities? If I can get the attention of the minister I should like to pursue this a little further.
Let us examine it in a little more detail. The offer under alternative B is such that there can be hardly any question but that Alberta will take alternative A. But if the application of B to Alberta were on the same basis as to the other provinces, namely, full payment of bond interest, there would be a much greater likelihood of Alberta taking B.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very little then.
Possibly it is a matter of balance and calculation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we paid the province on condition that they paid the bondholders, they would be worse off financially than if they accepted proposal A.

That is a matter of calculation. What I want this ministry to do is to declare whether they are going to condone the action of the Alberta government in withholding bond interest by paying it in full on the basis of their debt and not having the province of Alberta pay it over to the bondholders. That is what I want to know. What is going to happen? Surely, if Alberta chooses A because of the fact that B may be construed as being only an offer of reduced interest payments, the dominion by its action is in effect pushing the Premier of Alberta into alternative A and in that way is condoning Alberta's action.
Another approach to this problem may be stated thus:	The government of Canada is
imposing certain taxes upon the citizens of Alberta. I wish to speak to the people of Alberta to-night. In the case of the other provinces, the federal government is offering, as alternative B, to pay the whole of the province's interest bill, less any amount collected for succession duties and, I believe, deductions for sinking fund. In the case of Alberta it is thus offering to pay only half this interest bill, unless provision is made for the payment of the full bill. It is quite true, I think, that even if the whole interest were offered to Alberta under alternative B, the Alberta government might still choose alternative A. But if it did so, it would then be reasonably clear that it had not been sincere in saying that it was not paying interest in full because it could not do so, inasmuch as the means of doing so would be available to it. I think the house and the country should have an explicit statement from the Minister of Finance as to the policy of the government and as to what it proposes to do. I press the minister to give us this statement, either now or at a later stage in the proceedings.
I come now to another aspect of this matter which has to do with the municipalities in the provinces which may adopt this grant in lieu of income and corporation taxes. In those provinces in which there is, and has been for many years, a municipal income tax, the whole question is presently being explored. In New Brunswick the provincial government has called a meeting, to be held on Tuesday, June 3, with the representatives of all municipalities. From the minister's statement it is not quite clear that the municipalities, either by vacating voluntarily or by being obliged to vacate the income tax field as a result of legislation to be passed by the provincial government giving effect to the proposal, are to be protected from loss of revenue. This is most important to those municipalities which have depended heretofore to a considerable degree upon this source of revenue, and most particularly to the cities and larger towns in New Brunswick. While I am instructed that other smaller municipalities have had this power of assessing and levying income tax, it is true that until very recently most of them had not fully carried out the law, and only in recent years have they been looking to this field as a source of revenue.
I am instructed that a summary of the dominion tax proposals has been submitted to New Brunswick and other provinces in a similar position. This is a summary of the dominion's proposals to the provinces, such as I have indicated.
(1)	The provinces will collect the personal and corporation income taxes on incomes of the year 1940 and any arrears of taxes applicable to prior years.
(2)	The provinces will cancel their personal and corporation income taxes on incomes of the year 1941.
(3)	In the case of corporations whose fiscal year-ends do not coincide with the calendar year, the provinces will collect a tax on the proportionate amount of the income of the corporation which is applicable to the calendar year 1940. For example, if a corporation ended its year on January 31, 1941, the provinces would collect the provincial corporation income tax on eleven-twelfths of the corporation's profits for the year ending January 31, 1941. This agreement will synchronize with the increase of 10 per cent in the minimum rate of tax under the dominion Excess Profits Tax Act which will apply from January 1, 1941.
(4)	The provinces will refund to taxpayers the amount of any taxes which may have been collected already on 1941 incomes.
(5)	The provinces will collect any flat rate or specific taxes on corporations which became

a liability of the taxpayer as at or prior to December 31, 1940, irrespective of the date when payment is due. If they are not a liability of the taxpayer as at or prior to December 31, 1940, they will be cancelled by the provinces and not collected; if collected already, they will be refunded.
(6)	The general principles outlined under items 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 will apply upon the termination of the agreements with the provinces and the reintroduction of the provincial income and corporation taxes.
(7)	The annual payments by the dominion to the provinces will be paid on a quarterly basis.
