The total amount of all such deductions will be paid to the provinces on the termination of the agreement.
I know the minister's answer will be that he deals only with the provinces, but he certainly can make it a condition precedent to any agreement being reached that the benefits accruing to the provinces in lieu of the sums that the municipalities will be asked or may be compelled to give up shall definitely be passed on to the municipalities. He will say to me, I am sure, that he has no other thought in his mind. I say to him that that is not good enough, that we must have a definite statement that the municipalities will be absolutely protected under any agreement made with the provinces.
The municipalities are the creation of the provinces. Their jurisdiction to impose income tax is derived from the province. The province has the power and authority by legislation to take this jurisdiction away; and if it does so without making arrangements for proper compensation, the municipalities, in order to carry on their services and, with regard to the larger cities and towns, many of their social services, will be obliged to have recourse to an increased impost on real estate. I protest as vigorously as I know how against any such suggestion. Real estate to-day, and for many years, has been bearing an undue proportion of municipal taxation.
I invite the minister here and now to state definitely what his proposals are in respect of the municipalities and especially what he proposes to do to protect the municipalities to which I have referred.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to intervene in any quarrel between the federal government and the Premier of Ontario, but I wish to express some regret that such a situation has arisen and that it was not possible when the dominion-provincial conference met in January to continue its proceedings and arrive at certain conclusions. I believe that the Rowell-Sirois inquiry, as it was called, has given us probably more information regarding our dominion-provincial relationships than we could possibly have gleaned by the reading of many volumes. Out of that report there could have arisen a discussion, if the participants in the conference had wished, of any and every phase of our economic and social life. I thought it was regrettable that the conference did not proceed. I am not going to attempt to place the blame, but I say that had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) taken a more definite stand, the conference might have proceeded in spite of the fact that some of the provincial premiers were antagonistic to it.
I am also of opinion that it wras unfortunate that public opinion had not been prepared for that conference by fuller information being given as to what was in the Rowell-Sirois report. Had public opinion been better informed as to the purpose and need of the inquiry, I believe that the division which arose subsequently would not have been so acute.
One of the matters which is under discussion under this bill and which was dealt with by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) is, I think, a natural outcome of our federal system of government. That federal system was established in 1867 when problems such as marketing, unemployment relief and all the rest were virtually unknown as national problems. At that time they were problems largely for the individual communities themselves, and the communities pretty well took care of them. But the world has moved since 1867, and the experience that we are having in the Dominion of Canada is the experience of all federal states and federal governments in the last several decades. The United States has experienced much the same conflict between the powers of the various states and the federal government. Even Australia, the newest of the federal states, has been subjected to a good many strains in the past few years, and we are now experiencing something of that sort. It is regrettable that this difference between the province of Ontario and the dominion government has arisen on the clause contained in the bill before us. I can see no reason why the government of

Income War Tax Act
Canada should not tax non-resident holders of Canadian securities. After all, this war is being fought to save Canada from domination by those who would destroy every interest which these people have in the country in which we live. Consequently, it seems to me, if we are taxing our own people owning our own securities, we should tax also the securities held by others who are not resident in this dominion but who are benefiting from the defence of our institutions by the people of Canada at the present time. Therefore I am hoping that this difficulty which has arisen will be straightened out and that the tax will remain.
I should like to add my view to that of those who are suggesting that a conference should be held, not necessarily on the basis of the Sirois report, but founded upon the comprehensive inquiry and a wide consideration of problems which are arising now and will inevitably rise when the war ends. I fear for the post-war period unless some government- and it must be the federal government-has power to deal with the domestic issues which will emerge from the present war. Therefore I would add my support to those who suggest that a conference be called on the widest possible basis; and might I suggest that when such a. conference is called, participation should not be limited to persons representing various governments, but should include some representatives of the opposition groups in our legislatures, in order that any agreements arrived at will have some continuity and consistency of purpose, because, as I remarked a few moments ago, we as a dominion must have power to deal with dominion-wide problems-a power which in many respects does not lie at the moment with the dominion. I hope that some way will be found of ironing out the present difficulties between the province of Ontario and the federal government.
This bill contains a number of clauses. I am glad that the income tax schedules are on a graduated scale and that they rise in their imposition as they go upward in the scale. That is a good principle. We may have to take more later on from incomes in the higher brackets. I wish that more were being taken now, because, as I have often said, what counts is not the amount which the taxpayer pays, but the amount which he has left.
I do not wish to delay the house, because I believe these proposals received a pretty thorough discussion when they were before us in resolution form. I wish to protest again, however, although I suppose there is not much use in asking the minister to make a change at this stage, against the low exemptions in the national defence tax. The bill states that
the exemption for a single man shall be on an income of $660 a year; that upon an amount over that, 5 per cent will be taken, and that 5 per cent will be exacted from the income of a married man over S1,200 a year. Those exemptions are much too low. With the increase in the cost of living, and with all the calls which are being made upon everyone, including the low-paid workers, to contribute to various funds, the amount left is not sufficient to maintain anything approaching the standard of life which our own bureau of statistics has, on a number of occasions, laid down as a minimum. I should like to have seen the exemptions raised to $750 and $1,500 respectively; even then they would have been quite low.
With regard to the other parts of the bill, I have not very much to say, because the resolutions upon which the bill is based received consideration at various times when they were before the house, and at this late stage of the session it is useless to put up any long argument against portions of this measure. I hope that if the minister sticks to these exemptions, he will see his way clear, when the next budget is introduced, to raise them to some extent. I believe- he will be almost compelled to do so because, with the tremendous loans which we are raising and the enormous expenditures that are to be made this year, it seems inevitable that there will be some increase of prices, particularly if goods of various kinds become scarcer as a result of the necessities of the war situation. That is to say, the cost of living may rise, and the amount left over after paying these taxes will not be sufficient to maintain either single or married people.
With these few words I am going to leave the matter, because I do not think much is to be gained by bringing pressure to bear upon the minister after the resolutions have been adopted and the bill has been introduced in its present form.

Coming from a city which is paying very nearly one-third of the national income tax, I wish to occupy about five minutes, on behalf of trade and commerce, small wage-earners and those with fixed incomes, in a discussion of this particular bill.
The first part of this bill sets the rates of income tax on individuals, and I may say that the whole principle of the bill is involved on the second reading. Is the amount of money which this bill proposes to levy for the purposes of the war necessary? Is it not too much? Will it be well spent? Is it in the public interest, or of the war-Canada's only business that now counts-and will the effect of
Income War Tax Act

it be a restraint on those who are doing something for the country, the business community, trade and commerce? I say that the total amount of money which this bill is intended to raise is not needed for war purposes, and that half should be charged to capital instead of only one-third, and half raised from revenues.
The government proposes in the first schedule of the bill a tax on individuals. The original schedule has been repealed, and a new one subsituted, marking up everything from away down as low as S150, up to the top. It is the man with the fixed income, the white-collar worker and the industrial worker, who will have to pay a large part of these increases, as well as the more well to do who are also heavily taxed.
The exemptions are also reduced. Then there is the question of dependency. Many people would be on relief, and either this government or some other government would have to maintain them, were it not for the fact that some of their friends are taking care of them, and consequently are taxed for it ind their allowance therefor reduced to practically nothing in this bill. In my opinion, instead of collecting all this money, for the war and civil government, out of income and revenue, the government should make 50 per cent of it a charge on capital. In the last great war the United States'charged the cost of the war and of civil government to income and capital in the ratio of one-third to income and two-thirds to capital. There is a great amount of money in the banks and insurance companies; in fact, so much money that they cannot get more than a fraction of one per cent, or none at all, for it. I contend that Bill No. 87 takes altogether too much in one year out of income from the taxpayers of the country, when one considers other taxes, dominion, provincial and municipal, a burden which they cannot carry to-day.
No doubt the minister needs the money. He has to get it somehow, and the Canadian people will support him if they know that the money is for the war and is necessary. He has to get that money either from income or by borrowing, but in my opinion this bill is asking for too much from income, and the huge jump in schedules is far too great. It seems that we can afford the luxury of the party system, the league, and a duplicate railway system without any effort at coordination, and many other wasteful expenditures, and now the minister adds to the burden of the taxpayers this further imposition which he has brought down in Bill No. 87. For many years I have been urging reform in this direction. In fact, when the late Hon. J. A. Robb was Minister of Finance I urged, in a

motion discussed for a day, a reform in connection with income tax, to restore it to the municipalities. Prior to 1918 the income tax was the exclusive field of the municipalities, but in the great war it was taken away from them by the federal power. The higher federal power at that time promised that after the war this right would be restored to the municipalities, but the promise was never fulfilled.
From 1927 on, I have been urging reform in taxation. We are overgoverned and overtaxed, and reform in these respects, together with parliamentary, cabinet, constitution, law and taxation reform, should be made the subject matter of careful study on the part of the government. The income tax burden bears heavily on those with fixed income, both in private and in public office, and I do not know how long this will continue. I suggest that so far the minister has been using too many big-stick methods.
There is one feature that I commend, namely, with regard to rentals. The taxation on real estate is now on the net amount earned. The Victorian era built up assets for the future, and we are squandering them in various ways. In the early days of the Victorian era the people kept the state; now we are heading for an era where the state is keeping the majority of the people. The city of Toronto was the first to apply for the right to impose death duties, gasoline tax and other duties, and then it asked that income tax be restored to it. But the moment the municipalities discover a tax, the province appropriates it, and then the dominion comes along and takes away from the municipalities and the provinces this source of revenue and puts it into its own exchequer. This is what is being done in Bill No. 87. I am afraid this bill is a step in the wrong direction. It is placing too great a burden on those people who have very small holdings in property and wealth, and they will probably lose more than the country will gain.
In the early days when this was a young country every government encouraged saving and thrift among the people, with the result that the small wage-earner was able to buy a home or a small farm or a market garden. These savings became the small man's investment-small personal estate or real estate. It was all the capital that the small man had, savings that came from thrift, encouraged by all governments. But by successive inroads from taxation the right to hold and possess property has been taken away from the common, man-the farmer and the industrial worker. I am and always have been a supporter of income tax and death

Income War Tax Act
duties, but there is a wrong and a right principle involved, and I suggest that you can go too far in what you charge to income, instead of utilizing money that is lying idle in the banks and elsewhere- money which, as I said before, is not earning a fraction of one per cent. A large part of that money could be utilized for this fiscal year. Prior to the present year all governments in Canada have encouraged people in thrift, to accumulate small amounts of wealth and property, and this has been a means of building up the country. It developed men of character, stability and business ability who by their small savings and thrift could take care of their children and the thrifty man's children could inherit his savings instead of getting nothing. But what can people do when so much of our debt is charged to income instead of being fifty-fifty-50 per cent to income and 50 per cent to capital?
I have already referred to schedule A. I suggest	that	the	rate	therein	on the	lowbrackets	to $9,000	is altogether	too high	forthe small man when one considers the other taxes he has to pay. The minister is carrying on an expensive publicity campaign at the present time	in connection	with	thevictory	loan.	He is	asking	everyone	toinvest.	But	how	can	people	invest whena bill like this, and other measures, impose such burdens upon them. Before the war, the small business man and the artisan had made commitments on mortgages, on their homes and on life insurance policies; but what with income tax and other levies that have been added, nearly everything the small man earned has been invested and committed, so that to-day he has not a copper left to invest in this victory loan, as he would like to do. All the high pressure	publicity	to get	him in	will	not
amount to a snap of the finger as an inducement to people to invest, because ' their money has been spent, and allotted, although these honest people are eager and anxious to help.
I have urged the minister to consider a national moratorium with regard to mortgages, insurance and so forth. I have paid, like many others, by way of insurance more than I	shall get	out of	the policy,	andI shall continue paying as long as I live, without any remedies in a straight life policy.	The government	might	very	well
look into this question. The minister wishes to make a success of the victory loan. Well, the loan is linked up with this bill. There ought to be some principle by which a small wage-earner with a policy, if he has
kept up his insurance for five or six years, might be allowed to postpone the payment of premiums until after the war at the rate of interest paid on the victory loan so that he may have some small share of that loan.
So far as exemptions are concerned, I cannot see any reason for reducing them. It costs more now for a man to live than before the war. Some of these exemptions should be retained in the 'lower class of income. Dependency is another matter. The last one is double taxation. Where is all this going to end? There was a debate on the question the other night.
Another tax is on page 6 of the bill, sections 16 to IS, the tax on non-residents. I was talking to a business man from Cleveland the other day. The American people have put a good deal of money into buildings on Bay street in Toronto and other cities in Canada and around lake Erie and lake Ontario, and into large and small buildings in our cities. This tax on non-residents of fifteen per cent will, I believe, be a restraint on investments coming into the country, and so have a very serious effect for the remainder of the war and after the war on building construction, public and private bonds, if these investments are to be dried up. They saved the day in many of the cities along the lake Erie shore and western Ontario to the head of the lakes by these cities being able to get real money from across the border.
Real estate rentals will be taxed on a gross income basis; the net income would be the wiser basis. I ask the government not to go too far. I believe they went too far in this for the first year. I believe half the schedule for those under $8,000 or $9,000 wmuld have been right. If the government had made any real effort to take advantage of the lease-lend bill for the large amount of money to be provided by Canada under this budget for the war to protect the shores of the United States and our own neutrality in case America is attacked, they could have got a substantial relief on our income tax and the other taxes in this budget. I am sorry that the minister has not decided on monthly instalments. After all, the small wage-earner just gets his monthly cheque, and it would be far better if there was a provision for payment of this tax by equal monthly payments over twelve months in the year.
These matters I have raised are worthy of consideration, as the war is Canada's only business that counts, and the people will pay if they know it is needed.

If one thing more than another makes me sick, it is to hear Toronto complaining about how much any budget is going to cost it. After having lived on the rest of the country as richly as Toronto has for so long, it ill becomes any person speaking for Toronto to complain about taxation. The city of Toronto has more grasping, greedy, unctuous people in it than any other city in the world. That statement does not need to be agreed to by any person, but it is my opinion-
The most generous city in Canada.

That is a generous
remark which the generous hon. gentleman has made.
I had intended to speak for a few minutes with reference to the telegram read a short time ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the Premier of Ontario. I suppose sending that telegram was the right thing to do; anything at all tending to ease this situation was probably the right thing to do. Yet I doubt if it was really necessary to give the Premier of Ontario this cushion to fall upon. If the people of Ontario desire to have double taxation, it is entirely in their own hands. If they do not desire double taxation, they can make known their wishes to their premier and he can arrange that there shall not be double taxation. If, however, they desire it, we do not need to worry ourselves over it. You know, Mr. Speaker, I think the rest of Canada is getting somewhat sick of continually playing up to the Premier of Ontario and endeavouring to smooth and soothe him. I sometimes think our Prime Minister has turned the other cheek once, twice or three or four times too often to Ontario's premier, and it might now be a good idea if he would stop doing that and leave it to Ontario's premier to come to his senses by himself in quietness and without further urging. I have, however, no definite objection to the course that has been taken; I hope it works.
With relation to the 15 per cent tax on non-residents, I understand that the bondholder in the United States actually gets an exemption from his own government for any money he pays to the Canadian treasury. I happen to have a certain client out west who comes from Minneapolis, who pays a considerable sum of money in this way into the Canadian treasury. He is given full credit by the United States authorities for the money

that he pays into our treasury under this particular tax, 5 per cent as it was, 15 per cent as it appears to stand at the moment. In such circumstances there is not any person in the United States for whom the Premier of Ontario needs to fight. It is true that there will be certain persons in the United States, artificial persons, such as mutual companies, who may not pay any tax at all there, and therefore no exemption could be granted them by the United States for the taxes they pay here. These would seem to be the only taxpayers who would be in any way injured by this tax. As against that, however, we must remember that any Canadians who earn income in the same way in the United States do not pay 5 per cent, do not pay 15 per cent but pay 16i per cent. That is my information; If I am not correct I should like to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

There remain, then,
some bondholders outside Canada who claim the protection of the Premier of Ontario. There are those persons living in the Bahamas, Canadians who grew wealthy here and moved away in the hope of drawing money out of this country and not being taxed. They do not need our sympathy. There is nothing unjust to them about this tax. Those Canadians should be here standing shoulder to shoulder with their fellow-countrymen.
One other subject to which I should like to advert for a moment is this question of more and more and better and bigger conferences. I certainly would have no objection to more conferences if I could believe, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) seems to do, that they could do any good. But here is the position we are in to-day; the echo of the footsteps of the three wrecking premiers, men who came here and wrecked the conference, has only just ceased ringing in these halls. There would not be any use at all in this government calling them back at this time. Every person is entitled to his own opinion; the leader of the opposition seems to think we might effect something by recalling these men. But with all respect, I do not believe it. I do not believe it would be any use at all at this time for this government to call another meeting. The same people, or some of them, this time would probably only put their heads in the door and laugh and walk away.

Does the hon. member
suggest that the exchange of telegrams is a better method of reaching an agreement on this particular problem? Seeing that he is

Income War Tax Act
giving gratuitous advice to the province of Ontario, he might be good enough to answer that question.

With regard to that I
can give a categorical answer. Yes; I think that is the better way to try to reach an agreement. To have everything on record before the public in that way is decidedly better at the present time than to call another conference. I am not so sure that to-day's method will be successful, because I doubt if anything will be successful, with that man. But in any event I doubt if a conference would do any good, certainly not at this time. Should others desire a conference, I understand the door is wide open for them to have it. If there be any indication from the premiers of the provinces that they would like to confer, certainly this government would not stand in the way; nor do I think it should. The point at the moment simply is whether, at this time, this government could do any good in calling another conference.
There is the suggestion by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, that if there were a conference-and he said he thought there should be one-that it should be attended by the various opposition leaders, as well-

No,
thanks.

That is just the sort of difficulty I had in mind. The opposition leader who sits closest to me says, "No, thanks." We could not get very far with that kind of conference. We would probably get too many "no thank you's" from the invited ones. Moreover, if such a meeting were convened, we would have to consider whether the premiers of the provinces would be willing to come here and have representatives of the various oppositions speaking on equal terms with them in presenting the opinions of their respective provinces. I do not fancy that would net us anything.
It seems to me, with respect to the general subject of conferences, that the only thing we can do at the present time is to let the matter rest as it is, until some of those who wrecked the last conference show a change of heart. I should hope that before long that might come to pass, and I should think that so far as Ontario is concerned, the people of Ontario will see to it that such a change of heart does occur.

I must
express my regret and surprise that the Minister of Finance ignored the position I took and the request I made for a statement respecting the principle of the bill. I do not know whether he intended it as a discourtesy to me, but I certainly suggest I was entitled to a considered reply before the debate on second reading was closed. I am, however, charitable enough to think that perhaps the minister did not understand that that was expected of him, and I should hope that he would give a reply at a later stage.
While I am on my feet I would ask a question, as to why the two young ministers from Ontario have not had anything to say about this matter. These two gentlemen have been in the government now for about a year- and this is a matter of vital importance to Ontario, the province which they are supposed to represent. Are they tongue-tied or are they ham-strung?
Both.
That is the question I should like to put to the two new ministers from Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped the leader of the opposition would follow the good resolve he stated earlier in the debate this evening. He pointed out that he was desirous of showing a conciliatory manner, and that he did not wish to cause any trouble in what he described, I believe, as an embarrassing situation. In Saskatchewan are a number of aged people who lived for a number of years in the Yukon and then moved to the province. Although they have never resided outside Canada, they are not eligible for an old age pension because apparently residence in the Yukon is not considered as being residence in any province. Under the agreements made between the dominion and the provinces, no province will take the responsibility for the payment of the dominion's share of 25 per cent of the pension in addition to their 75 per cent. In my opinion this ought to be ironed out. The hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black) will be better informed about this, but it may be that those who live in the Yukon have other ways of providing for old age.
I have in mind one case of a man whose wife resided in Saskatchewan for a number of years, but he did not establish domicile in the province to come within the meaning of the act. For a time he did get an old age pension, but he was cut off and has had to repay the overpayment made. Because of his residence in the Yukon it was considered to have been an improper payment. The Minister of Mines and Resources is in charge of Yukon affairs, and I suggest to him that some consideration should be given to this point. There are many cases of real hardship. This one old gentleman has suffered because he has been unable to get a sufficient pension, and even when he did get one for a while because the provincial authorities thought they were justified in paying it, he has since had to suffer a reduction to repay the overpayment. I ask the minister to consider these cases and endeavour to find some way to provide for these people, either through his department, or through the Old Age Pensions Act under the Department of Finance by fgreement with the territorial administrator.

Supply-Parks and Forests Branch

The Old Age Pensions Act does not apply to the Yukon. No arrangement has been made between the federal government and the territorial government similar to the agreements entered into with the various provinces. At present the dominion government pays 75 per cent of the pension paid, while the provincial government pays 25 per cent. In my opinion, this whole matter should be a federal responsibility, and residence in Canada should be the ground upon which a pension is paid. I must say that men and women who are no longer able to take care of themselves are treated more generously in the Yukon than they are in the other provinces. A pension of $20 a month would be of no use to anyone living in the Yukon because of the much higher costs of living. I agree, however, with the hon. member who has just spoken, that many hardships have been caused where people have left the Yukon after living there some years. A man may live in the Yukon for ten years and then move to Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia. If he gets a pension, it is based upon the length of his residence in the province. As I say, this should be a federal responsibility, and residence in any part of Canada should be the governing factor.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) has moved to reduce this vote of $50,000 by $2,5u0. I happen to know why the Minister of Mines and Resources wants to have this vote reduced. I am aware that later on a similar amount will be provided in the supplementary estimates to be devoted to a certain purpose. I commend the minister for taking action in a deserving case. Compensation of at least some $2,500 is to be paid to a father for the loss of his son while a passenger on a government owned and operated ferryboat in the Yukon territory. The law is such that this man was precluded from going even to the exchequer court in order to establish his rights. The matter was considered by the Minister of Mines and Resources and the Department of Justice, and this grant of $2,500 is to be made and will, I know, be gratefully received.
I suggest to the minister that it might be well for him or some member of his staff to intimate to the comptroller of the Yukon and the council the inadvisability and impropriety of voting money on the strength of the federal estimates before these estimates become, in fact, votes or grants of money. The passing of any item in the estimates is a speculation. The fact that it is in the estimates does not mean that inevitably there is going to be a grant and I think these expectant recipients of public money should 14873-215}
not presume to appropriate it or begin to expend it before it is granted by vote of this parliament on the advice of the respective ministers.
I have not taken up very much of the time of the house at this session, but since this is a vote to the government of the Yukon territory, perhaps it would not be out of place if I had a word to say about the Yukon. Probably there are not very many members of this house who know much about that far-distant territory. I shall not weary them with statistics but touch on just a few of the highlights.
To begin with, the Yukon has an area of 207,076 square miles and a population of little over 5,000 people. That means there are forty square miles to every one of the population. Consequently we are not overcrowded.
The Yukon was created a separate territory, carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1898, by the Yukon Act, which is the constitution of that territory. We were given a local government, consisting now of a comptroller appointed by the dominion government, and a territorial council or legislature consisting of three members, one from each of the three electoral districts in the territory. That council with the comptroller has practically the powers of a provincial legislature. Under the Yukon Act they can legislate concerning many matters including property and civil rights, and the members of this house well know how far that goes. When a legislature has the power to legislate on property and civil rights, there is practically nothing on earth that it cannot do.
We were given representation in Canada by a special act called the Yukon Representation Act. Never, even at that time when the population of Yukon was much greater than it is now, did we have a sufficient population to entitle us to representation in parliament. But because of the importance of the territory as a market for Canadian goods and its great gold production, all governments have continued the policy of keeping the Yukon represented in this parliament. Local laws are passed by that local council to govern local matters. Our mining laws, on the contrary, are all acts of this parliament of Canada.
Originally the mining laws of the Yukon were orders in council subject to change overnight, and they were changed in many instances without notice to the mine owners and others interested in the mines, with the result that we had a state of chaos there and a multiplicity of lawsuits. Once we got representation in parliament, it was not long before that condition of affairs was changed, and

Supply-Parks and Forests Branch
stable and permanent mining laws which can only be altered by an act of this parliament were enacted and are in force.
As a member of that local council I had the honour of assisting in drafting what is known as the Yukon Placer Gold Mining Act, and then of coming to parliament as the Yukon's representative. I had the duty of drafting, with the approval, support and assistance of the Hon. Charles Stewart, then Minister of the Interior, the bill which was enacted by this parliament and became the law of the Yukon, known as the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. To arrive at the terms of those acts as to both placer gold mining and lode mineral mining, meetings of the miners, both employers and employees, were held all over that territory, of men who came from all parts of the world where mining is done. Their views were heard and their suggestions taken and boiled down, and out of those conferences these acts of parliament became the law of the land.
The principal mining business of the Yukon is the mining of gold, as well as the mining of silver and lead. Last year the Yukon produced 108,077 ounces of a monetary value of $3,782,726, an increase over the year before of 17,568 ounces, of a value of about $615,000. The total amount credited in the public accounts of Canada to the Yukon as having been collected as royalties on gold mines up to March 31, 1940, amounted to $5,197,123.
Originally a royalty of 10 per cent on the gross output of gold was charged. That was afterwards reduced to 5 per cent, and the rate is now 2J per cent on the gross output. The royalty is now paid by the transfer of the gold into cash at the various banks, and the banks see to it that the royalty is paid. Formerly gold was collected by royalty collectors who went from mining claim to mining claim and collected the gold in specie, gold dust, gold nuggets and gold.
Knowing the conditions that existed up in that country at that time and the strange things that happened under the midnight sun, I feel that there was a great deal collected that never found its way into the books of the receiver general of Canada, and that if all the royalties on gold collected had gone into the public accounts and into the public treasury, the Yukon would be credited with an amount far greater than $5,197,123.
Extensive deposits of galena ore are known to exist in the Yukon, galena being a combination of silver and lead, and many millions of dollars have been produced in mining that area. The chief operator in silver lead mines is the Treadwell Yukon corporation

which has mined with great success and profit and paid the federal government substantial returns in taxation based on profits.
The system of taxation on lode mines is a graded system of taxation on profits. On placer gold the tax is on the gross output, regardless of profit or loss. That company buys hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of Canadian goods and pays substantial sums into the federal treasury in excise and customs duties. But the Yukon does not get credit for that, because the great bulk of its purchases are made at the city of Vancouver and that port of customs gets credit for them. These things are overlooked when people remark as to whether the Yukon is a bill of expense or profit to the dominion. Those of us in the Yukon who can be classed as old-timers appreciate the improved conditions in that territory, not only in the system and methods of government but in the conditions of life generally. We have seen transportation in that country progress from the dog team and canoe to steamboats and railways, and now we have a splendid aeroplane service carried on by the British-Yukon Navigation company, a British company with a fleet of passenger boats, a railway, and a fleet of up-to-date aeroplanes.
The Yukon also produces a considerable amount of fur, upon which, too, the government levies a tax.
Lode mining in Yukon began on an extensive scale as late as 1939, when the first gold brick was poured. In 1940, 1,147 ounces of gold were produced by that method. The remoteness of the country and the expense of equipment have made capital slow in investing in that far-distant land, but I have no doubt that eventually lode mining will be one of the great industries of the Yukon. In passing, I should like to pay a tribute to one gentleman of the geological survey parties which the minister sends up to the Yukon each year, namely, Doctor Bostock, who is most attentive and considerate in his attitude towards the miners in that country. He spares no time or effort in visiting and examining mining properties, giving the prospectors valuable advice as to formations and methods. Speaking for Yukoners, I may say that they are always pleased to see him come.
By those not familiar with the facts, the Yukon has been looked upon as nothing but a bill of expense to Canada, without adequate revenues and returns. In the early days that may have been true; but even then, if credit had been given for its value as a market for Canadian goods, and the government's returns in gold royalties, customs and other sources of revenue had been taken into

Supply-Parks and Forests Branch
account, I am of opinion that it would not have been in the red on that account. To-day the Yukon undoubtedly pays its way so far as the cost of administration is concerned.
The public accounts show that the federal revenues in the Yukon during the past fiscal year amounted to 8349,252. In addition to that, the revenues of the territorial government were 8153,485. The federal government expended $478,310, showing a surplus, taking into account the two governments, of $24,427. In addition to that, the federal government has large revenues from the Yukon business from which the Yukon gets no credit. As I said before, the Yukon buys the bulk of its goods in Vancouver. Let us for a moment take the approximate figures for four of the chief buyers of goods in the Yukon. First, the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation, an English company mining placer gold in an up-to-date way, paid last year, on goods purchased in Canada and imported to the Yukon, sales and excise taxes of $60,000 and cutoms duties of $30,000, plus income tax for which I have no figures; and last year they paid out $1,260,300 in wages in that territory. The sums of $60,000 and $30,000 which I have mentioned were paid to the collectors of taxes at Vancouver, British Columbia, and not into the Yukon. Take the Treadwell Yukon Corporation, a silver-lead mining company They paid in the same year in the same sort of taxes, $80,000. One firm of merchants having trading posts throughout the territory paid in the same sort of taxes, $10,000. In the case of another commerical company I have the figures for only two of its depots, where it paid in taxes, $32,410. The total in respect of the four companies I have mentioned is $212,410, all from Yukon companies, and all paid into the treasury through the port of Vancouver, British Columbia. I am confident that on careful examination a much larger amount could be credited to the Yukon; probably it would run as high as $300,000.
Or consider the figures of collections made in the Yukon. For the past fiscal year the customs, excise and income taxes amounted to $214,160. For the last fiscal year the income tax was $90,530, and for the nine months of the present fiscal year, 1940-41, it is $181,171, an increase of over 100 per cent in the nine months of this year. Post office revenues have increased steadily in each of the past ten years. Yukoners import all their clothing, all their machinery, all their tools, most of their timber and practically all of their food. They produce little but gold, silver, lead and fur.
The cost of all federal services in the Yukon is played up in the public accounts. For instance, if you turn to the item which the
committee will be considering before long, namely, the expense of administration of the Department of Indian Affairs, you find that it cost Canada this year $5,465,187. Of that amount, the cost of maintaining Indians in the Yukon was less than $50,000. No particular mention is made of what it costs in the various provinces, but the Yukon is singled out as a horrible example of government expense.
Turn to an item in the estimates for the maintenance of a telegraph service. It is listed, northern British Columbia and Yukon, $129,508. Inquiry shows that $107,508 is spent in British Columbia and only $22,000 in the Yukon.
Or take the federal grants for mining roads. Last year they amounted to $1,208,920. Where did that money go? Quebec got $245,000; Ontario, $245,000; British Columbia, $240,000; Manitoba, $210,000; Saskatchewan, $130,000; the Yukon, less than $40,000.
Hon. members may have observed that I have made these rather voluminous notes on material which comes to me through the mail from the director of public information. In passing, may I remark, with all due respect, that the money which is expended on the department of public information is not well spent. Reams of so-called information come through the mail to every hon. member, although any items of interest may be found in the daily newspapers or heard over the radio. In my opinion it is a waste of money, salaries, time and material.
Another project which is of great interest to the Yukon is the Alaska highway. Various routes have been reported on to this government by an international committee. It is estimated by that committee that the cost of the Canadian section will be $25,000,000. That is for an unpaved, dirt road. Any hon. member who has had experience in government expenditures knows that when they say it will cost $25,000,000,. you will not be far wrong if you say that it will require double that amount, or $50,000,000. We have had experience of the great difference between the estimates of what a public work will cost and what it actually costs. Older members will recall the estimates submitted for the construction of that famous bridge across the St. Lawrence. It cost millions more than was estimated. Take the construction of what is now the Canadian National Railways. At the outset, that was not estimated to cost Canada much more than $15,000,000. Everyone knows that it cost hundreds of millions, and to-day we have unfortunately an unnecessary duplication of railway service over thousands of miles of the country. All the traffic, passenger,

Supply-Parks and Forests Branch
freight and express could be handled by one road. Take another instance of estimates being away under actual cost of construction. Take that monument to unnecessary and ill-advised expenditure, the Hudson Bay railway. That was not going to cost much. What has it cost?
With regard to the Alaska highway, we should not lose sight of the fact that the mileage of that road through Canada-British Columbia and the Yukon-will far exceed the mileage necessary to build the Alaska road. The road when built must of necessity go through the Yukon. As a Yukoner, representing the Yukon in this house, I might be said to be disloyal to the Yukon if I did not advocate the building of that road. But, as a Canadian, I say that the money of the taxpayers should not at this time be spent on that project, nor should money be spent at this time on the completion of the railway terminal at Montreal. Neither project will help in winning the war; and unless we win this war, what use will any of these projects be to any of us? If the United States want a highway to Alaska across British Columbia and Yukon, and are willing to bear the expense of building and maintaining it, I am all for it. Let them come. Encourage them to come and do it. In view of the friendly relations which now exist, and which have existed for so many years between that great republic and Canada, which friendly relations, I am free to admit, have recently been so palpably strengthened and further cemented by the diplomacy of the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), Canada should not hesitate to allow the United States at their own expense to construct and maintain that highway across western Canada to their territory of Alaska.
In normal times, with prosperity prevailing in Canada, I would not make that suggestion. I should prefer to have Canada build and maintain the Canadian section of that road. There is, however, no discounting the fact that we have not now the money with which to do it. It may be said that Canada is prosperous. Perhaps it is by comparison with some countries of the world, many of which, instead of enjoying prosperity, are enduring slavery, degradation, poverty, misery and want under the heel of their savage conquerers. If it is suggested that Canada is prosperous, we know it is to a large extent false prosperity, built on the exchange among our people of huge sums of money being taken away from them in many forms of taxation, and some paid back to them for lands, goods, high salaries, services and labour said to be needed in this war. That spending has created a
[Mr. G. Black.)
boom; but there will come an end to all that, and we should face the future and anticipate the return to normal life and business. Meantime, I say that, apart from war expenditures, only those expenditures that are absolutely needed should be made now. The construction at this time in Canada by Canada of the Alaska highway is not one of those necessary expenditures.
For a moment may I refer to the recruiting campaign. The Minister of National Defence very properly suggests that members of parliament should help. They should help, and I for one will help. But when one approaches a young healthy man of war age and suggests that lie should join the army, the navy or the air force, and one gets this reply: "I will, if John Doe or Richard Rowe or somebody else will, but why should I go and let them step into my job that pays me well, while I go and fight for them?"- that is a hard question to answer. The word "conscription." meaning compulsory military service, is taboo. Why? Every member of this house knows why. It is for political reasons and nothing else. Leaders of both great Canadian political parties in the last election pledged those parties against conscription; but notwithstanding the fact that the leader of the party I have supported took that attitude, I did not hesitate during that campaign to say publicly, as I say now, that in my opinion the only fair and just way to raise an army is by compulsion. Capital owes a debt to the state. It is compelled by law to contribute the sinews of war; it is compelled by taxation. It would be as reasonable to say that only those who volunteer to do so should pay income tax. The payment of income tax, the payment of any tax, is the performance of a duty to the state, the payment of a debt to the state. All fit young men in Canada owe to the state a debt which can be paid only by their entry into the fighting forces. If they join voluntarily, so much the better; all honour to them for it. But if they fail in that duty, if they fail to pay that debt which they owe their country, they like the taxpayer should be made to pay. It is manifestly unfair to carry on recruiting in any other way.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture the other day declare among other things that conscientious objectors will be put into labour camps. I suggest to him that he ought to go further. I suggest that conscientious objectors so-called, Doukhobors, Mennonites, Hitterites and Dunkers, should be disfranchised federally, provincially and municipally; and when the time comes, their property acquired in this free Canada of ours

Supply-Parks and Forests Branch
should be taken from them at a fair price, and they should be sent back to the country whence they came. I do not think there is such a thing as a conscientious objector. That is a hypocritical objection. I suggest to the minister that in supplying these so-called conscientious objectors with picks, shovels and board and lodging, he equip them with foot-warmers. It is their cold feet that bother them, not their consciences.
To get back to the Yukon, we have there a splendid system of public schools, good hospitals, enough churches. The people have comfortable homes and fine families. On the whole, the people are industrious, prosperous, happy and contented. They realize that they are going through this life only once, and what they have here they cannot take with them, so that they make the best of it while they have it. I must pay a tribute to the women of the Yukon. Even in normal peace times the consideration they show those in need because of illness, old age or hard luck is remarkable. In this war, as in the last, they have been doing magnificent work in the Red Cross and the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire, and have made large quantities of useful clothing and sent them to Canadians overseas and to the suffering people of England. I am happy to say that, per capita, the Yukon purchases of war savings certificates were greater than those of any province in the dominion.
In passing, may I say a word about that splendid force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Ever since the Yukon was the Yukon, that is the force in which the people have had unbounded confidence and to which they have looked up as being responsible for law and' order prevailing in that territory. They exercise their power in a commonsense way and with discretion.
Although I sit on the left of Mr. Speaker, I believe in giving credit where credit is due, and I congratulate the Minister of Mines and Resources and those of his staff who take part in the administration of the government of the Yukon. It is an economical businesslike government and a pattern for many if not all of the provincial governments. In fact, the dominion government might very well take a leaf out of the Yukon book as to methods of government. For the most part the Yukon government gets a dollar's worth for every dollar spent, and I doubt whether many members of this house can say that is so of governments in those parts of Canada from which they come. I support the minister's motion to vote this sum, and I only regret that it is not a much larger one.
Amendment agreed to.

I should like to make a brief remark on the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when the item was called. Hon. members are aware that the federal government does not pay old age pensions. Old age pensions originate in the provinces and are paid by the provinces, and the federal government makes a contribution to the amount paid.
Of 75 per cent, is it not?

Yes, 75 per cent. If, for instance, there were a province that did not initiate and pay old age pensions, no old age pensions would be paid in that province by the federal government. The Yukon territory is in a sense similar to a province. It has a territorial government which operates under an act of parliament, and it is really a matter for the Yukon territorial council, which is an elective body, to initiate old age pensions. It has the power to do so, I understand, should the council in its wisdom decide it to be advisable.
And if it did, the federal government would make the same contribution of 75 per cent?

I have no doubt the federal government would make the same contribution.
I appreciate very much what the hon. member, who represents in this house,-very worthily, may I say,-'the Yukon territory, has said this evening. I value the compliment he has paid to the Yukon administration. It is due almost entirely to the character and efficiency of the officers of the department who have to do with the administration. We endeavour, so far as possible, to- have that administration efficient, economical and worthy of the territory. Usually we get brick-bats from the opposition instead of bouquets; to-night I have had a bouquet, and I thank my hon. friend for it.
Item as amended agreed to.
1S5. Lands, parks and forests branch. Eastern arctic expedition, $25,700.
Does this item include the cost of sending the Nascopie into the Arctic?
Yes. My hon. friend has stated correctly what the item is. It is to care for disbursements in sending the Nascopie to the far northern and eastern arctic, which is done once every year.

Does the Nascopie carry geologists or mining engineers to survey or discover evidences of mineral along the trip?
Victory Loan

Not many mining engineers or geologists make the trip on the Nascopie. I believe there have been a few occasions when that has been done. There are studies conducted by scientists in other fields, and they of course make their journey to the eastern arctic by this boat. In addition, the boat transports the mounted police who may be going to relieve detachments which have been on duty at the various outlying posts, takes in supplies, medical doctors and nurses who may be going to replace others coming out. It is the general service for all the government departments in the eastern arctic that comes under this vote.

Item agreed to.
lSJ/. Lands, parks and forests branch. Government of the Northwest Territories-general administration, operation and maintenance of services, including Wood Buffalo park, $266,655.

reference to Yukon affairs there is due to the fact that the secretary performs dual functions. We have head office administration for the Yukon territory as well.
